title: 4  Utility, Risk and Decisions
text:
4.6 Nash Equilibrium
When multiple decision makers interact with each other, meaning the decision of one player changes the state of the “world” and thus affects the decision of another player, then we need to consider the notion of equilibrium. It is a central concept in economics and game theory. The most widely used type of equilibrium is the Nash equilibrium, named after John Nash, who introduced it in his 1950 paper “Equilibrium Points in N-Person Games.” It was popularized by the 2001 film “A Beautiful Mind,” which depicted Nash’s life and work.
It is defined as a set of strategies where no player can improve their payoff by unilaterally changing their strategy, assuming others keep their strategies constant.
Here are a few examples of Nash equilibria:

Prisoner’s Dilemma: Two prisoners must decide whether to cooperate with each other or defect. The Nash equilibrium is for both to defect, even though they would be better off if they both cooperated.
Pricing Strategies: Firms in a market choose prices to maximize profits, taking into account their competitors’ pricing decisions. The equilibrium is the set of prices where no firm can increase profits by changing its price unilaterally.
Traffic Flow: Drivers choose routes to minimize travel time, based on their expectations of other drivers’ choices. The equilibrium is the pattern of traffic flow where no driver can reduce their travel time by choosing a different route.


Example 4.14 (Marble Game) Here is a subtle marble game where players have to call out (or present) either red or blue with different payoffs according to how things match. Two players \(A\) and \(B\) have both a red and a blue marble. They present one marble to each other. The payoff table is as follows:

If both present red, \(A\) wins $3.
If both present blue, \(A\) wins $1.
If the colors do not match, \(B\) wins $2

Nobody pays the other player, so the game is not zero-sum.
The question is whether it is better to be \(A\) or \(B\) or does it matter? Moreover, what kind of strategy should you play? A lot depends on how much credit you give your opponent. A lot of empirical research was done on the tit-for-tat strategy, where you cooperate until your opponent defects. Then you match his last response.
Nash equilibrium will also allow us to study the concept of a randomized strategy (ie. picking a choice with a certain probability) which turns out to be optimal in many game theory problems.
First, assume that the players have a \(\frac{1}{2}\) probability of playing Red or Blue. Thus each player has the same expected payoff \(E(A) = \$1\) \[\begin{align*}
    E(A) &= \frac{1}{4} \cdot 3 + \frac{1}{4} \cdot 1 =1 \\
    E(B) &= \frac{1}{4} \cdot 2 + \frac{1}{4} \cdot 2 =1
\end{align*}\] We might go one step further and look at the risk and calculate the variances of each player’s payouts. \[\begin{align*}
    Var (A) & = (1-1)^2 \cdot \frac{1}{4} +(3-1)^2 \cdot \frac{1}{4} + (0-1)^2 \cdot \frac{1}{2} = 1.5 \\
    Var(B) & = 1^2 \cdot \frac{1}{2} + (2-1)^2 \cdot \frac{1}{2} = 1
\end{align*}\] Therefore, under this scenario, if you are risk averse, player \(B\) position is favored.
The matrix of probabilities with equally likely choices is given by



\(A,B\)
Probability




\(P( red, red )\)
(1/2)(1/2)=1/4


\(P( red, blue )\)
(1/2)(1/2)=1/4


\(P( blue, red )\)
(1/2)(1/2)=1/4


\(P( blue, blue )\)
(1/2)(1/2)=1/4



Now there is no reason to assume ahead of time that the players will decide to play \(50/50\). We will show that there’s a mixed strategy (randomized) that is a Nash equilibrium that is, both players won’t deviate from the strategy. We’ll prove that the following equilibrium happens:

\(A\) plays Red with probability 1/2 and blue 1/2
\(B\) plays Red with probability 1/4 and blue 3/4

In this case, the expected payoff to playing Red equals that of playing Blue for each player. We can simply calculate: \(A\)’s expected payoff is 3/4 and \(B\)’s is $1 \[
E(A) = \frac{1}{8} \cdot 3 + \frac{3}{8} \cdot 1 = \frac{3}{4}
\] Moreover, \(E(B) =1\), thus \(E(B) > E(A)\). We see that \(B\) is the favored position. It is clear that if I know that you are going to play this strategy and vice versa, neither of us will deviate from this strategy, hence the Nash equilibrium concept.
Nash equilibrium probabilities are: \(p=P( A \; red )= 1/2, p_1 = P( B \; red ) = 1/4\) with payout matrix



\(A,B\)
Probability




\(P( red, red )\)
(1/2)(1/4)=1/8


\(P( red, blue )\)
(1/2)(3/4)=3/8


\(P( blue, red )\)
(1/2)(1/4)=1/8


\(P( blue, blue )\)
(1/2)(3/4)=3/8



We have general payoff probabilities: \(p=P( A \; red ), p_1 = P( B \; red )\)
\[\begin{align*}
    f_A ( p , p_1 ) =& 3 p p_1 + ( 1 -p ) ( 1 - p_1 ) \\
    f_B ( p , p_1 ) =& 2 \{ p(1 - p_1) + ( 1 -p ) p_1 \}
\end{align*}\]
To find the equilibrium point \[\begin{align*}
    ( \partial / \partial p ) f_A ( p , p_1 ) =& 3 p_1 - ( 1 - p_1 ) = 4 p_1 -1 \; \; \mathrm{so} \; \; p_1= 1/4 \\
    ( \partial / \partial p_1 ) f_B ( p , p_1 ) =& 2 ( 1 - 2p ) \; \; \mathrm{so} \; \; p= 1/2
\end{align*}\]
Much research has been directed to repeated games versus the one-shot game and is too large a topic to discuss further. However, we can analyze one particularly famous strategy: tit-for-tat.
In a repeated version of the marble game (Camerer 2003), player \(A\) can employ the tit-for-tat strategy: start by playing Red in the first round, and thereafter simply repeat the opponent’s previous move. This strategy was famously shown by Robert Axelrod in his computer tournaments to be remarkably effective in iterated prisoner’s dilemma games, despite its simplicity.
Consider player \(A\) using tit-for-tat against various strategies employed by \(B\).
If \(B\) always plays Red, the game locks into a mutually beneficial pattern: both players present Red every round, and \(A\) wins $3 each time. The per-round expected payoff for \(A\) is simply $3.
If \(B\) always plays Blue, the dynamics are more interesting. In round 1, \(A\) plays Red while \(B\) plays Blue, so the colors mismatch and \(B\) collects $2 while \(A\) collects nothing. From round 2 onward, \(A\) copies \(B\)’s Blue, resulting in both playing Blue and \(A\) winning $1 per round. Over \(n\) rounds, \(A\)’s total payoff is \(0 + (n-1) \cdot 1 = n - 1\), giving an average of \((n-1)/n\) which approaches $1 as \(n \to \infty\).
If both players use tit-for-tat starting with Red, they remain synchronized forever, each playing Red in every round, yielding $3 per round for \(A\). This mutual cooperation is stable because neither player ever defects.
The more challenging case arises when \(B\) employs an alternating strategy. Suppose \(B\) plays Red, Blue, Red, Blue, and so on. Then the sequence unfolds as follows: in round 1, \((A,B) = (R,R)\) so \(A\) wins $3; in round 2, \(A\) copies \(B\)’s Red while \(B\) switches to Blue, giving \((R,B)\) and \(B\) wins $2; in round 3, \(A\) copies Blue while \(B\) plays Red, giving \((B,R)\) and \(B\) wins $2; this pattern of \(B\) winning $2 continues indefinitely. After the first round, tit-for-tat becomes permanently out of phase with the alternating opponent, and \(A\) never collects again: the cumulative payoff freezes at the $3 won in round 1.





Cumulative payoff for player A using tit-for-tat against different opponent strategies over 50 rounds. The curves for Always Red and Tit-for-Tat coincide on the top line.




The simulation reveals that tit-for-tat performs excellently against cooperative or consistent opponents, collecting the full $3 every round against Always Red and against another tit-for-tat player. Those two cases are in fact the same series: both settle into mutual Red from the opening round, so the curves coincide exactly; the figure draws Always Red as a wide light line and Tit-for-Tat as a dashed dark line on top of it. Against random play tit-for-tat averages about $1 per round, which is precisely the one-shot value \(E(A)=1\) computed earlier. The reason is that copying a random opponent reproduces its previous draw, which matches the current one half the time, and a match is equally likely to be red-red or blue-blue, giving \(\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{2}\cdot 3 + \frac{1}{2}\cdot 1)=1\). It does worst against the alternating strategy, which exploits the one-round lag inherent in the copying mechanism and holds \(A\) to nothing after the opening round.

Average Payoff

The key insight from Axelrod’s tournaments was that tit-for-tat succeeds not by exploiting opponents, but by fostering cooperation. It is nice (never defects first), retaliatory (punishes defection immediately), forgiving (returns to cooperation if the opponent does), and clear (easy for opponents to understand and predict). These properties make it robust in environments where opponents can learn and adapt, even though it can be exploited by adversaries who know the strategy and deliberately play to keep it out of phase.
Thomas Schelling, in his influential essay The Manipulation of Risk, extends these game-theoretic insights to international relations, arguing that conflicts between major powers often resemble what he calls competitions in risk-taking or tests of nerve rather than direct tests of force. In this framing, the marble game captures something essential about diplomacy: outcomes are determined not by who can bring the most force to bear, but by who is willing to escalate further or who can make it appear that escalation is forthcoming.
Schelling emphasizes the central role of face in such interactions, though he uses the term carefully. Face is not mere pride or status; it is a country’s (or player’s) reputation for action, the expectations others hold about how it will behave in future encounters. As Schelling puts it, face is the interdependence of a country’s commitments. When player \(A\) in our marble game employs tit-for-tat and retaliates against defection, \(A\) is not merely responding to the current round but preserving expectations about future behavior. If \(A\) were to let defections pass unpunished, \(B\) would rationally update beliefs about what \(A\) will tolerate, potentially inviting further exploitation.
This perspective illuminates why tit-for-tat’s retaliatory property is so important: it maintains credibility. Schelling notes that it would be hard to persuade an adversary, if one yielded repeatedly on minor issues, that one would stand firm on a vital issue. The same logic applies in repeated games: a player who fails to punish defection signals weakness, inviting further defection. Yet Schelling also cautions that face should not attach itself to unworthy enterprises, and that it is sometimes wise to help an adversary save face by providing an exit that does not appear to be capitulation. In game-theoretic terms, this suggests that optimal strategies in repeated interactions must balance retaliation with opportunities for returning to cooperation, precisely the forgiving quality that makes tit-for-tat effective.

Equilibrium analysis helps predict the likely outcomes of strategic interactions, even when individuals are acting in their own self-interest. Further, we can use it to understand how markets function and how firms make pricing and production decisions or to design mechanisms (e.g., auctions, voting systems) that incentivize desired behavior and achieve efficient outcomes.
One major drawback is that equilibrium analysis relies on assumptions about rationality and common knowledge of preferences and strategies, which may not always hold in real-world situations. Furthermore, some games may have multiple equilibria, making it difficult to predict which one will be reached. The problem of dynamic strategies, when individuals may learn and adjust their strategies as they gain experience, is hard.

Exercise 4.2 (How Accurate Must the Newcomb Demon Be?) Consider a general version of Newcomb’s problem (Example 4.2). The opaque box contains \(M\) dollars if the demon predicted one-boxing and \(0\) otherwise; the transparent box always holds \(k\) dollars, with \(0 < k < M\). The demon predicts correctly with probability \(1-\varepsilon\), so \(\prob{\text{demon predicts option}_i \mid \text{option}_i} = 1-\varepsilon\) for \(\varepsilon \in [0, 1/2]\).

Write the conditional expected payoff of one-boxing and of two-boxing as functions of \(\varepsilon\), \(M\), and \(k\).
Solve for the threshold \(\varepsilon^\star\) at which the two conditional expected payoffs are equal, and show that \(\varepsilon^\star = \tfrac12\left(1 - k/M\right)\).
Evaluate \(\varepsilon^\star\) for the book’s numbers, \(M = \$1{,}000{,}000\) and \(k = \$1{,}000\). How accurate must the demon be before conditional expected utility favors one-boxing?
The dominance argument for two-boxing does not depend on \(\varepsilon\) at all: two-boxing yields \(k\) more than one-boxing for any fixed content of the opaque box. Reconcile this with your answer to (c). Under what assumption about the relationship between your choice and the box’s content does the dominance argument’s silence on \(\varepsilon\) stop being a strength and become a weakness? Relate your answer to the distinction between causal and evidential decision theory discussed in the chapter.



Exercise 4.3 (Resolving Ellsberg with Ambiguity Aversion) Recall the Ellsberg setup (Example 4.6): urn A holds 50 red and 50 black balls; urn B holds 100 balls in an unknown red/black mix. Suppose all you are told about urn B is that its probability of drawing red, \(p\), satisfies \(p \in [0.3, 0.7]\), with no information about where in that range \(p\) lies. Each bet pays $1 if the named color is drawn and $0 otherwise.

Show algebraically that no single value of \(p \in [0.3, 0.7]\) can simultaneously make \(\E{\text{1A}} > \E{\text{1B}}\) and \(\E{\text{2A}} > \E{\text{2B}}\) under ordinary (single-prior) expected utility, reproducing the chapter’s contradiction.
Now suppose the decision maker evaluates a bet on urn B by its worst case over the ambiguity set: its value is \(\min_{p \in [0.3,0.7]}\) of its expected payoff, computed separately for each bet. Compute the maxmin value of bet 1B and of bet 2B, and compare each to the (unambiguous) value of the corresponding bet on urn A.
Show that under the maxmin criterion both \(\text{1A} \succ \text{1B}\) and \(\text{2A} \succ \text{2B}\) hold at once with no contradiction, and explain in a sentence why maxmin escapes the argument in (a) even though it never assigns urn B a single probability.
Consider instead a symmetric ambiguity interval \([0.5 - \delta,\, 0.5 + \delta]\) for \(\delta \in (0, 0.5]\). Show that maxmin predicts strict ambiguity aversion (both A-bets strictly preferred) for every such \(\delta\), and describe what happens as \(\delta \to 0\).

0.2




Calculate \(E(X)\), the expected number of people who will attend.
The owner of the venue is going to charge you $1500 for rental and other miscellaneous costs. You know that you will make a profit (after per person costs) of $40 for each person attending. Calculate the expected profit after the rental cost.
The owner of the venue proposes an alternative pricing scheme. Instead of charging $1500, she will charge you either $5 per person or $2100, whichever is smaller. So if 100 people come, you only pay $500. If 500 come, you pay $2100. Calculate the expected profit under this scheme (still assuming $40 per plate profit before you pay the owner).
Let \(Y_1\) be your profit under the first scheme, and \(Y_2\) be your profit under the second. If you do the calculations, it turns out that the standard deviations of these profits are: \[\sigma_{Y_1} = 4996 \qquad \sigma_{Y_2} = 4488\] Using the expected values calculated above, explain which of the two scenarios you prefer.



Exercise 4.5 (Marjorie Visit) Marjorie is worried about whether it is safe to visit a vulnerable relative during a pandemic. She is considering whether to take an at-home test for the virus before visiting her relative. Assume the test has sensitivity 85% and specificity 92%. That is, the probability that the test will be positive is about 85% if an individual is infected with the virus, and the probability that test will be negative is about 92% if an individual is not infected.
Further, assume the following losses for Marjorie



Event
Loss




Visit relative, not infected
0


Visit relative, infected
100


Do not visit relative, not infected
1


Do not visit relative, infected
5




Assume that about 2 in every 1,000 persons in the population is currently infected. What is the posterior probability that an individual with a positive test has the disease?
Suppose case counts have decreased substantially to about 15 in 100,000. What is the posterior probability that an individual with a positive test has the disease?
Suppose Marjorie is deciding whether to visit her relative and if so whether to test for the disease before visiting. If the prior probability that Marjorie has the disease is 200 in 100,000, find the policy that minimizes expected loss. That is, given each of the possible test results, should Marjorie visit her relative? Find the expected value of sample information (EVSI), the reduction in expected loss from having the test. Repeat for a prior probability of 15 in 100,000. Discuss.
For the decision of whether Marjorie should visit her relative, find the range of prior probabilities for which taking the at-home test results in lower expected loss than ignoring or not taking the test (assuming the test is free). Discuss your results.



Exercise 4.6 (The Winner’s Curse: Conditioning on Actually Winning) Return to the claiming-race setup of Example 4.8: a horse’s true value \(V\) is $0 (never wins) or $50,000 (improves), each with prior probability \(1/2\), and the claiming price is a fixed $20,000. Before deciding whether to claim, you receive a private scouting signal \(S \in \{\text{Buy}, \text{Pass}\}\) with \(\prob{S = \text{Buy} \mid V = 50{,}000} = 0.9\) and \(\prob{S = \text{Buy} \mid V = 0} = 0.2\).

Using Bayes’ rule, compute \(\prob{V = 50{,}000 \mid S = \text{Buy}}\) and \(\E{V \mid S = \text{Buy}}\). Judging by your own signal alone, does claiming look profitable?
Suppose exactly one rival claimant observes an independent signal with the same accuracies, conditionally independent of yours given \(V\). Institutional rules award you the horse only if you signal Buy and your rival signals Pass; call this event \(W\) (you win). Compute \(\prob{W \mid V = 50{,}000}\), \(\prob{W \mid V = 0}\), and hence \(\prob{V = 50{,}000 \mid W}\) and \(\E{V \mid W}\).
Compare (a) and (b). Once you correctly condition on actually winning rather than on your own signal alone, does claiming still look profitable? Explain in words why the two calculations differ.
Now suppose the signal is symmetric: \[
\prob{S = \text{Buy} \mid V = 50{,}000} = \prob{S = \text{Pass} \mid V = 0} = q
\] for some \(q \in (0,1)\). Show that \(\prob{V = 50{,}000 \mid W} = 1/2\) for every \(q\). Explain intuitively why a symmetric scouting signal leaves you no net information once you condition on winning, however accurate it is.



Exercise 4.7 (Minimax versus Bayes Risk) Consider a decision problem with two possible states of nature, \(\theta_1\) and \(\theta_2\), and two available actions, \(a_1\) and \(a_2\), with loss table

Let \(\pi = \prob{\theta_1}\) and \(1-\pi = \prob{\theta_2}\) be a prior on the two states. Write the Bayes risk \(r(\pi,a_i) = \E[\pi]{\mathcal{L}(\theta,a_i)}\) of each action as a function of \(\pi\). Find Bayes’ rule (the action with the smaller Bayes risk) and the Bayes risk under the prior \(\pi = 0.5\).
Repeat part (a) for the prior \(\pi = 0.2\).
Find the least favorable prior \(\pi^\star\): the value of \(\pi\) at which \(r(\pi,a_1) = r(\pi,a_2)\), so the statistician is indifferent between the two actions. What is the common Bayes risk at \(\pi^\star\)?
Now restrict attention to pure (non-randomized) minimax decisions: for each action compute its worst-case risk \(\max_\theta \mathcal{L}(\theta,a_i)\), and choose the action that minimizes this worst-case risk. Is the resulting minimax risk the same as the Bayes risk you found at \(\pi^\star\) in part (c)?
Suppose instead the statistician may randomize, choosing \(a_1\) with probability \(q\) and \(a_2\) with probability \(1-q\). Find the value of \(q\) that minimizes the worst-case (over \(\theta\)) expected loss, and show that at this \(q\) the resulting rule has the same expected loss regardless of which state is true (an equalizer rule). Compare this randomized minimax value to your answers in (c) and (d). When does the (possibly randomized) minimax rule coincide with Bayes’ rule against the least favorable prior?



Exercise 4.8 (Eliciting a CRRA Utility Function) Recall the CRRA (constant relative risk aversion) utility family from Example 4.3, \(U_\gamma(w) = \dfrac{w^{1-\gamma}-1}{1-\gamma}\) for \(\gamma\neq 1\), with \(U_1(w)=\log(w)\). A subject with current wealth \(\$100{,}000\) is offered a fair coin-flip gamble: with probability \(1/2\) her wealth becomes \(\$150{,}000\), and with probability \(1/2\) it becomes \(\$50{,}000\). She states that she is indifferent between taking this gamble and simply receiving \(\$75{,}000\) for certain, so her certainty equivalent for the gamble is \(CE=\$75{,}000\).

For a 50/50 gamble between wealth levels \(w_1\) and \(w_2\), show that the CRRA certainty equivalent, defined by \(U_\gamma(CE) = \tfrac12 U_\gamma(w_1) + \tfrac12 U_\gamma(w_2)\), satisfies \[
CE(\gamma) = \left(\tfrac12 w_1^{1-\gamma} + \tfrac12 w_2^{1-\gamma}\right)^{1/(1-\gamma)}, \qquad \gamma\neq 1,
\] and that \(CE(1) = \sqrt{w_1 w_2}\) under log utility. [Hint: \(CE(\gamma)\) is a power mean of \(w_1,w_2\) of order \(1-\gamma\).]
Using \(w_1=50{,}000\) and \(w_2=150{,}000\), show that \(\gamma=2\) exactly rationalizes the subject’s stated certainty equivalent of \(\$75{,}000\). [Hint: for \(\gamma=2\), part (a)’s formula reduces to a familiar named average of \(w_1\) and \(w_2\).]
Using the elicited \(\gamma=2\), predict this subject’s certainty equivalent for a new 50/50 gamble between \(\$60{,}000\) and \(\$300{,}000\). What risk premium (expected wealth minus \(CE\)) does this imply?
The arithmetic, geometric, and harmonic means of two positive numbers always satisfy \(\text{AM}\geq\text{GM}\geq\text{HM}\), with equality only when \(w_1=w_2\). Using part (a), explain why this inequality guarantees that, for any fixed 50/50 gamble, the certainty equivalent must (weakly) decrease as \(\gamma\) increases through \(0\) (risk neutral), \(1\) (log utility), and \(2\). Verify this ordering numerically for both gambles in this problem.



Exercise 4.9 (The St. Petersburg Paradox and Bounded Utility) Consider a modified St. Petersburg game (compare Example 4.1): a fair coin is flipped until the first head appears, on flip \(N\). Instead of the payoff \(2^N\) from the chapter, this casino pays \(X=3^N\) dollars.

Show that the expected monetary payoff \(\E{X}\) diverges. More generally, for a payoff \(X=c^N\) with \(c>1\), show that \(\E{X}\) diverges whenever \(c\geq 2\), and converges to a finite value when \(1<c<2\) (find that value).
For \(c=3\), using log utility \(U(x)=\log(x)\), find the certain dollar amount \(x^\star\) (the certainty equivalent) that gives the same expected utility as playing this game. [Hint: you will need \(\E{N} = \sum_{k=1}^\infty k(1/2)^k\); recall \(\sum_{k=1}^\infty kx^k = x/(1-x)^2\) for \(|x|<1\).] Show more generally that for a payoff \(c^N\), the log-utility certainty equivalent is \(x^\star=c^2\), so the classical game (\(c=2\)) recovers the chapter’s \(x^\star=4\).
Bounded utility is often cited as the fully general resolution of St. Petersburg-type paradoxes. If \(U\) is bounded above (say \(U(x)\le M\) for every payoff \(x\) in the support of \(X\)), explain why \(\E{U(X)}\) is finite no matter how fast the payoffs \(X\) grow, so a finite certainty equivalent always exists.
Log utility is unbounded above, so it cannot be a fully general fix, only a fix for games that do not grow too fast. Show this concretely using the following “Super-St. Petersburg” payoff, due to the mathematician Karl Menger (1934): \(X=2^{2^N}\). Show that even \(\E{\log X}\) diverges, so log utility fails to resolve this faster-growing paradox, while a bounded utility function still would (by part c).



Exercise 4.10 (Mixed-Strategy Equilibrium in a Token Game) Consider a variant of the marble game of Example 4.14. Players \(A\) and \(B\) each secretly present one of two tokens, Sun or Moon. If both present Sun, \(A\) wins $5; if both present Moon, \(A\) wins $2; if the tokens differ, \(B\) wins $3 (and \(A\) wins nothing). Let \(p = \prob{A \text{ plays Sun}}\) and \(p_1 = \prob{B \text{ plays Sun}}\).

Following the chapter’s derivation for the marble game, write \(A\)’s and \(B\)’s expected-payoff functions \(f_A(p, p_1)\) and \(f_B(p, p_1)\).
Find the mixed-strategy Nash equilibrium \((p^\star, p_1^\star)\) two ways: (i) by setting \(\partial f_A/\partial p = 0\) and \(\partial f_B/\partial p_1 = 0\) as in the chapter, and (ii) directly, by requiring each player be indifferent between their two pure actions given the other’s equilibrium mixture. Confirm the two methods agree.
Compute each player’s expected payoff at \((p^\star, p_1^\star)\). Which player is favored, and does the direction match the book’s original marble game?
Now modify the game so that a mismatch pays \(B\) different amounts: \(B\) wins $3 when \(A\) shows Sun and \(B\) shows Moon, but \(B\) wins $5 when \(A\) shows Moon and \(B\) shows Sun (all matching payoffs unchanged). Recompute the equilibrium. Which player’s equilibrium mixing probability changes and which stays the same? Explain, in terms of whose indifference condition pins down which probability, why a change to \(B\)’s payoffs shifts \(A\)’s equilibrium probability rather than \(B\)’s.




Computing

Exercise 4.11 (Certainty Equivalent and Risk Premium) Return to the fundraiser dinner of the “Decisions” exercise above. Attendance \(X\) takes values \(100, 200, 300, 400, 500\) with probabilities \(0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.2, 0.2\), and profit under the flat-fee rental scheme is \(Y_1 = 40X - 1500\), with \(\E{Y_1} = 11{,}300\). A risk-neutral organizer values the dinner at \(\E{Y_1}\), but a risk-averse organizer values it less. Suppose the organizer’s preferences follow a CARA (constant absolute risk aversion) utility function \[
u(w) = \frac{1 - e^{-aw}}{a}, \qquad a > 0,
\] where the coefficient \(a = -u''(w)/u'(w)\) is the (constant) coefficient of absolute risk aversion.

Write an R function for \(u(w,a)\) and compute the expected utility \(\E{u(Y_1)}\) for \(a = 0.0002\).
The certainty equivalent \(CE\) is the sure amount satisfying \(u(CE) = \E{u(Y_1)}\). Show that \[
CE = -\frac{1}{a}\log\left(1 - a\,\E{u(Y_1)}\right),
\] and compute \(CE\) and the risk premium \(\E{Y_1} - CE\) for \(a = 0.0002\).
Compute \(CE(a)\) over a grid of \(a\) from near \(0\) to \(0.0015\) and plot the risk premium \(\E{Y_1} - CE(a)\) against \(a\). What happens to the risk premium as \(a \to 0\)? As \(a\) grows, what value does \(CE\) approach, and why does that make sense?



Exercise 4.12 (The Kelly Criterion and Long-Run Growth) Consider a favorable repeated bet, in the spirit of Example 4.4: at each round you wager a fraction \(f\in(0,1)\) of your current wealth. With probability \(p\) you win, and your wealth is multiplied by \(1+bf\) (the wager is returned along with \(b\) times its size as profit); with probability \(q=1-p\) you lose, and your wealth is multiplied by \(1-f\). Take \(p=0.4\) and \(b=2\) (a “2 to 1” payout), so the bet has a positive edge per dollar wagered, \(pb-q = 0.4(2)-0.6=0.2\).

Show that the expected log-growth rate of wealth per round is \[
G(f) = p\log(1+bf) + q\log(1-f),
\] and, by solving \(G'(f)=0\), derive the optimal (full-Kelly) fraction \(f^\star = p - q/b\). Verify \(G''(f)<0\) everywhere, confirming this is a maximum, and evaluate \(f^\star\) numerically for \(p=0.4, b=2\).
In R, define G(f) and confirm numerically, by a grid search or optimize(), that its maximizer matches your formula for \(f^\star\).
Simulate \(N=5{,}000\) independent paths of \(T=200\) bets each, starting from wealth \(W_0=1\), for three betting fractions: full Kelly \(f^\star\), half Kelly \(f^\star/2\), and an over-betting fraction \(3f^\star\). Report, for each fraction, the median terminal wealth, the median terminal log-wealth, and the ruin frequency, defined as the fraction of paths whose wealth ever drops below \(1\%\) of \(W_0\). Set a seed.
Compare \(\text{median}(\log W_T)/T\) from your simulation to the theoretical \(G(f)\) from part (a) for each fraction. Discuss the trade-off between growth rate and ruin risk as you move from half-Kelly to full-Kelly to over-betting.



Exercise 4.13 (Value of Information: EVPI and EVSI) An energy company must decide whether to drill an exploratory well at a new site (all payoffs below are in $ millions). If oil is present, drilling yields a net payoff of \(40\); if the site is dry, drilling yields a net payoff of \(-10\) (the sunk cost of drilling with no return); not drilling always yields \(0\) regardless of the true state. A geological assessment gives a prior probability \(\prob{\text{Oil}} = 0.3\).

Using the prior alone, find the expected monetary value (EMV) of the optimal decision (drill or do not drill), with no additional information.
The expected value of perfect information (EVPI) is the expected payoff if the company could learn the true state before deciding, minus the EMV from part (a). Compute EVPI in R and interpret it as the maximum amount worth paying for a perfect signal about the site.
A seismic survey is available, with \(\prob{\text{Positive}\mid\text{Oil}} = 0.80\) and \(\prob{\text{Negative}\mid\text{Dry}} = 0.75\); the survey costs \(2\) ($ million). In R, compute \(\prob{\text{Positive}}\) and \(\prob{\text{Negative}}\), the posterior probability of oil given each result, the optimal action and its expected payoff given each result, the overall expected value with sample information, and the EVSI (that value minus the EMV of part (a), before subtracting the survey’s cost). Should the company purchase the survey?
Confirm numerically that \(0\leq\text{EVSI}\leq\text{EVPI}\). Then run a Monte Carlo check of your analytic EVSI: simulate the true state, the (correlated) test result, and the resulting test-contingent decision for a large number of draws, and compare the simulated average payoff to your analytic answer. Explain intuitively why a perfect signal can never be worth less than an imperfect one about the same uncertainty.

When a complete sufficient statistic exists, the Lehmann-Scheffé theorem (Lehmann and Scheffé 1950) shows that an unbiased function of it is the unique minimum variance unbiased estimator.↩︎

title: 5  A/B Testing
text:
5.1 Hypothesis Testing
The Internet age opened the door to enormous data collection on personal preferences, behaviors, and actions. The data collected are observational rather than data collected from designed experiments, where we can control the environment to find the effects of interventions. User interface design is a prime example of this. Companies like Google, Amazon, and Netflix run thousands of experiments a year (Kohavi, Tang, and Xu 2020) to optimize user experience and revenue. A/B testing is essentially a randomized controlled trial at scale, where two variants (A and B) are compared to determine which one performs better on a specific metric. The statistical machinery remains the same: we formulate a null hypothesis (no difference between variants), collect data, and compute a statistic to see if the observed difference is significant or just noise. The A/B variations can be physical, such as different colors or layouts, or they can be algorithmic, such as different search algorithms or recommendation systems.
However, a key distinction exists between traditional scientific hypothesis testing and modern A/B testing: the objective. In scientific research, the primary goal is often truth discovery, establishing a reproducible fact about the world. This necessitates a conservative approach with strict control over False Positives (Type I errors). In contrast, the goal of A/B testing in industry is often decision making, choosing the best option to maximize a business metric like revenue or engagement. Here, the cost of a missed opportunity (Type II error) can be just as detrimental as a false alarm. Consequently, industry practitioners may focus more on the magnitude of the effect (effect size) and the expected value of the decision, rather than relying solely on a rigid \(p\)-value threshold.
Throughout this chapter, we use the classical testing language as an operational planning tool: Type I and Type II errors and significance levels. In particular, \(\alpha\) denotes a frequentist Type I error rate (test size). Chapter 6 revisits the same problems from a Bayesian decision-theoretic viewpoint, where posterior probabilities, Bayes factors, and explicit losses take center stage; when we discuss credibility or posterior uncertainty, we will avoid overloading \(\alpha\) with a second meaning.
How do we know if the difference between variants is real or just noise? Consider a coin flip: if it comes up heads twice in a row, is the coin biased? Obviously two tosses aren’t enough to tell. Hypothesis testing formalizes this intuition: it tells us whether we have enough evidence to draw a conclusion, or whether we need more data.
You work as a quant for a trading firm, and you have developed a new algorithm to trade stocks. You tested your algorithm on historical data, and it outperformed the existing algorithm used in your company. Now, the important question is whether your trading strategy can truly outperform the market or it just got lucky. We need to analyze the performance of the algorithm after it was created and decide whether we have truly discovered a dominant strategy. The effect we try to measure is usually present in some statistics that we calculate from data, for example, sample mean, proportion, or difference in means.

title: 5  A/B Testing
text:
Example 5.1 (Pyx Trial) The “Pyx Trial” refers to an ancient ceremony of the United Kingdom’s Royal Mint. This tradition, dating back to the 12th century, is a method of testing the quality of minted coins to ensure it meets the standards of weight and purity set by law. The term “Pyx” comes from the Greek word “pyxis,” meaning a small box, which is used to hold the sample coins that are to be tested (Stigler 1977).
Sir Isaac Newton became Warden of the Mint in 1696 and later the Master of the Mint. His role was central to reforming the coinage and improving its quality. Newton was rigorous in enforcing standards and combating counterfeiting and clipping (the practice of shaving off small amounts of precious metal from coins). Newton applied his scientific mind to the problems of minting, including refining assays (the testing of the purity of metals), improving the design of coins to prevent clipping, and overseeing the recoinage of 1696 into milled coin.
The trial starts by selecting \(n\) coins from each batch produced by the Royal Mint. These coins are placed in a box called the Pyx. The number of coins used in the Trial of the Pyx can vary each year and depends on several factors, including the variety and quantity of coins produced by the Royal Mint in that particular year. Typically, a representative sample of each type of coin minted is selected for testing. Then, for each coin attribute (weight, size, composition), the mean (average) value of the sample is calculated and compared with the legal standard, and the variance of the mean tells us how far it can stray by chance alone.
Suppose we have minted one million coins and collected the sample of \(n=100\) coins, the legal weight tolerance for a certain coin is 0.05 grams.
We will use the simulated data for our analysis. Let’s simulate the weights of all of the coins produced

set.seed(17) # Kharlamov
allcoins <- runif(1000000, 4.95, 5.05)

Now, we sample 100 coins at random

survey_sample <- sample(allcoins, size = 100, replace = FALSE)
xbar <- mean(survey_sample)

The sample mean of 4.9950764 is very close to the true mean of 5. However, if we were to collect a different sample, the sample mean would be slightly different.
A second sample gives a sample mean of 5.002014. Now, we simulate 2000 samples and calculate the sample mean for each sample.

prep <- replicate(2000, mean(sample(allcoins, size = 100, replace = FALSE)))
hist(prep, breaks = 30, freq = F, main = "", xlab = "Sample mean weight (grams)", col = "lightblue")
p <- seq(4.9, 5.1, length.out = 500)
lines(p, dnorm(p, mean(prep), sd(prep)), col = "red", lwd = 3)




Histogram of sample means from 2000 simulated samples.




We see that the bell-curve (normal density) is a good model for the distribution over the means calculated from samples. In fact, the central limit theorem says that, for large samples, sample means approximately follow a normal distribution. We need to estimate the mean and standard deviation of this bell curve. It is natural to use the sample mean as the estimate of the mean of the bell curve mean(prep): 4.9998448. The mean \[
\bar x = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i
\] is close to the true population mean of 5. We sometimes use the notation \(\hat \mu\) to denote an estimate. So we have \(\hat \mu = \bar x\).
However, the standard deviation is much lower compared to the standard deviation of the population

sd(prep)
## 0.0028
sd(allcoins)
## 0.029

The variance of the mean measures how much the sample mean is expected to vary from one sample to another, if you were to take multiple samples from the same population.
Assuming that samples are uncorrelated (correct sampling procedure is important!), the variance of the mean is given by \[
\Var{\bar X} = \Var{\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i} = \frac{1}{n^2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \Var{X_i} = \frac{\sigma^2}{n}.
\]
Therefore, the variance of the mean formula is \[
\Var{\bar X} = \frac{\sigma^2}{n}.
\] If we know the population variance \(\Var{X_i} = \sigma^2\), then we can calculate the variance of the mean. However, in practice, we do not know the population variance. Instead, we estimate it using the sample variance \(s^2\). The estimated variance of the mean is then \[
\widehat{\text{Var}}(\bar X) = \frac{s^2}{n}.
\] The standard deviation of the mean is called the standard error and is given by \[
s_{\bar X} = \sqrt{\widehat{\text{Var}}(\bar X)} = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}.
\]
Let’s compare the standard error of the mean and standard deviation calculated from the simulations

sd(prep)
## 0.0028
sd(allcoins) / sqrt(100)
## 0.0029

They are very close!
This statistical property allows us to quantify uncertainty about the sample mean and say something about the true value of the mean \(\mu\), in terms of a probabilistic interval statement.


Central Limit Theorem
CLT states that, given a sufficiently large sample size, the distribution of the means of i.i.d. observations with finite variance will be approximately normally distributed, regardless of the shape of the population distribution. This normal distribution is also known as the Gaussian distribution. The theorem applies to a wide range of population distributions, including distributions that are not normal. This universality underlies its central role in statistics.
The Central Limit Theorem originates from the De Moivre-Laplace theorem, published by de Moivre in 1738, which established the normal approximation to the binomial distribution. According to this theorem, the standard normal distribution arises as the limit of scaled and centered Binomial distributions, in the following sense. Let \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) be independent, identically distributed Rademacher random variables, that is, independent random variables with distribution \[
P(X_i = 1) = P(X_i = -1) = \frac{1}{2}.
\] Then, the distribution of the sum of these random variables, divided by \(\sqrt{n}\), converges to the standard normal distribution as \(n\) tends to infinity. That is, for any \(a<b\), we have \[
\lim_{n\to\infty} P\left(a \le \frac{X_1+\cdots+X_n}{\sqrt{n}} \le b\right) = \int_a^b \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-x^2/2} dx.
\] More generally, for i.i.d. summands with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\), the sum \(X_1+\cdots+X_n\) has mean \(n\mu\) and variance \(n\sigma^2\), so that the standardized sum \((X_1+\cdots+X_n - n\mu)/\sqrt{n\sigma^2}\) has mean \(0\) and variance \(1\). The theorem then states that the distribution of this standardized sum converges to the standard normal distribution as \(n\) tends to infinity.
Francis Galton devised a mechanical illustration of this limit, now called the Galton board, and described it in his book Natural Inheritance (Galton 1889). A ball dropped at the top of the board meets one pin in every row of pins, is deflected to the left or to the right, and comes to rest in one of the bins at the bottom. Consider a board with 12 rows. At each pin the ball takes a \(\text{Bernoulli}(1/2)\) step, equal to 1 when it goes right and 0 when it goes left, and each row contributes one such step as a summand. The bin of a ball is its number of right steps, a sum of 12 independent steps, so the bin follows a \(\text{Binomial}(12, 1/2)\) distribution with mean \(12/2 = 6\) and variance \(12/4 = 3\). The code below drops 1000 balls through such a board, draws the number of balls in each bin as bars, and adds the normal density with the same mean and variance, scaled to counts. Already with 12 rows, the bar heights follow the normal curve of the central limit theorem closely (Figure 5.1).

set.seed(1889)
n <- 1000
rows <- 12
steps <- matrix(rbinom(n * rows, 1, 0.5), n, rows)
bin <- rowSums(steps)
hist(bin, breaks = seq(-0.5, rows + 0.5), main = "", col = "gray80",
     xlab = "Bin (number of right steps)", ylab = "Number of balls",
     ylim = c(0, 250))
curve(n * dnorm(x, rows / 2, sqrt(rows / 4)), add = TRUE, lwd = 2)







Figure 5.1: A simulated Galton board with 12 rows of pins and 1000 balls. The bars show the number of balls in each bin and the curve is the normal density with mean 6 and variance 3, scaled to counts.






Example 5.2 (Android Earthquake Alerts) A modern example of the idea behind the Central Limit Theorem, that pooling many noisy and weak signals gives a strong one, is Google’s Android Earthquake Alerts System. The core idea is to use the accelerometers present in Android smartphones to create a global earthquake detection network.
Each individual phone’s accelerometer is a “noisy sensor.” It can be triggered by many events that are not earthquakes, such as the phone being dropped, vibrations from a passing truck, or even loud music. A signal from a single phone is therefore a “weak signal”: on its own, it’s not reliable enough to issue an earthquake alert.
However, Google’s system aggregates signals from a large number of phones in a specific geographic area. When a real earthquake occurs, many phones in the affected region will detect the seismic waves at roughly the same time.
By pooling the reports from this large number of sensors, the system can effectively cancel out the random noise from individual phones. A single phone dropping is a random, isolated event. But thousands of phones vibrating in a synchronized pattern is a clear, strong signal that is highly unlikely to be due to chance.
This illustrates the principle that the standard error of a mean is inversely proportional to the square root of the sample size (\(s_{\bar X} = s/\sqrt{n}\)): the more phones, the smaller the chance fluctuation of what they report jointly. This allows the system to have a high level of confidence that the detected event is a real earthquake, enabling it to send out timely alerts to people who may be in danger.

title: 5  A/B Testing
text:
5.2 Confidence Intervals
The fact that the distribution of the simulated means from the Pyx example can be described well by a normal bell curve has a theoretical justification in the Central Limit Theorem above.
There are a few conditions. The sampled observations must be independent. In practice, this means that the sampling should be random, and one observation should not influence another. Further, the sample size should be sufficiently large. While there is no strict rule for what constitutes “large enough,” a common guideline is a sample size of 30 or more. However, if the population distribution is far from normal, a larger sample size may be required.
We can estimate the mean of this bell curve using \(\bar x\) and the standard deviation (standard error) using \(s/\sqrt{n}\).
The square-root nature of this relation is somewhat unfortunate. To halve the standard error of the mean, you need to quadruple the sample size.
One of the main applications of this result is the construction of confidence intervals. A confidence interval is a range of values that is likely to contain the true value of the population mean. The 95% confidence interval is calculated using the sample mean \(\bar x\) and the standard error \(s/\sqrt{n}\) as follows \[
\bar x \pm 1.96s_{\bar X}, ~ s_{\bar X} = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}.
\]
Here are a few conclusions we can make thus far

Mean estimates are based on random samples and therefore random (uncertain) themselves
We need to account for this uncertainty!
Standard Error measures the uncertainty of an estimate
Using properties of the Normal distribution, we can construct \(95\)% Confidence Intervals
This provides us with a plausible range for the quantity we are trying to estimate.

Recall the Patriots coin toss example from Chapter 1, we know that they won 19 out of 25 tosses during the 2014–2015 season. In this example, our observations are values 0 (lost toss) and 1 (won toss), and the average over those 0-1 observations is called the proportion and is denoted by \(\hat p\) instead of \(\bar x\). When we deal with proportions, we can estimate the variance of the proportion from \(\hat p\) as follows \[
s^2_{\hat p} = \frac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{n}.
\] Thus, we know that given our observations and CLT, the sampling distribution of our estimator \(\hat{p}\) is approximately normal (written \(\overset{\cdot}{\sim}\)). Our best guess at the mean \(p\) is \(19/25 = 0.76\) and at the variance \(s^2 = 0.76(1-0.76)/25 = 0.0073\) \[
\hat p \overset{\cdot}{\sim} N(p, 0.0073).
\] Then a \(95\%\) Confidence Interval is calculated by

0.76 + c(-1.96, 1.96) * sqrt(0.0073)
## 0.59 0.93

Since 0.5 is outside the confidence interval, we have enough evidence to say that the coin tosses were not fair. (The Patriots were singled out after the fact, which is the multiple testing issue of Section 5.4.1.)
Our status-quo assumption (there is no effect) is called the null hypothesis and is typically denoted by \(H_0\).

Mythbusters Example
While A/B testing is industry-standard for software, the same methodology applies to testing physical phenomena or human behavior, dealing with small sample sizes where uncertainty is higher. In 2006 the creators of Mythbusters TV show on Discovery channel wanted to test whether yawning is contagious in humans. They recruited 50 participants and each of those went through an interview. At the end of 34 randomly selected interviews, the interviewer did yawn. Then participants were asked to wait in a next-door room. Out of 34 participants from the experimental group, 10 did yawn (29.4%), and only 4 out of 16 (25%) in the control group did yawn. The difference in the proportion of those who did yawn was 4.4%. The show hosts Kari Byron, Tory Belleci and Scottie Chapman concluded that yawn is indeed contagious.
To translate the question from this experiment into language of hypothesis testing, we say that our null hypothesis is that the proportion of yawning participants in the control group (\(p_c\)) and in the experimental group (\(p_e\)) is the same, \(H_0: p_c - p_e = 0\), and the alternative hypothesis is \(H_1: p_c < p_e\). Hypotheses are always statements about the population proportions \(p_c\) and \(p_e\), never about the sample estimates \(\hat p_c\) and \(\hat p_e\), which are what we observe. The goal is to use the data to tell us if the hypothesis is correct or not.
A key statistical fact behind the hypothesis testing is the Central Limit Theorem. It states that if we have a sample \(\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\) with \(n\) i.i.d. observations from any distribution with finite mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\), then for large \(n\) the average of the sample approximately follows a Normal distribution with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2/n\) \[
\bar X = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_i \overset{\cdot}{\sim} N(\mu, \sigma^2/n)
\]
Let us use a simple simulated dataset to demonstrate the central limit theorem. We generate 100 outcomes of a Bernoulli trial with \(p=0.3\) and calculate the mean of this sample \(\hat p\). We repeat it 2000 times and compare the empirical distribution of \(\hat p\) with \(N(0.3, 0.046^2)\).

set.seed(1)
a <- replicate(2000, mean(rbinom(100, 1, 0.3)))
plot(density(a), main = "", xlab = expression(hat(p)))
se <- sqrt(0.3 * (1 - 0.3) / 100) #  0.046
x <- seq(0, 0.5, length.out = 300)
lines(x, dnorm(x, mean = 0.3, sd = se), col = "red", lwd = 3)
legend("topright", c("simulated", "normal approximation"), col = c("black", "red"), lwd = c(1, 3), bty = "n", cex = 0.7)








There are three ways to quantify uncertainty in hypothesis testing. The first approach relies on calculating confidence intervals, as we will do for the yawn example in Example 5.9. There are two complementary approaches. One is to calculate what is called a \(p\)-value, that is the probability of a result at least as extreme as the one observed in the data, assuming the null hypothesis is true. If \(p\)-value is low, then we reject the null-hypothesis. For the yawn example, the conditional probability that the observed difference in proportions is greater than 0.044, given null hypothesis is true is given by
\[
p\text{-value} = P(\hat p_e - \hat p_c \ge 0.044 \mid H_0),
\] which can be calculated using pnorm function, with the variance 0.0177 of the difference derived in Example 5.9

1 - pnorm(0.044, 0, sqrt(0.0177))
## 0.37

The \(p\)-value of 0.37 means that there is a 37% chance to observe the difference to be greater than 0.044 assuming the null-hypothesis. It is quite high! We want the \(p\)-value to be low, only then we can claim that we have discovered a new fact, i.e., that yawning is contagious. In many applications we require this number to be at most 0.05. This cut-off is called the significance level and is typically denoted as \(\alpha\). We can test the hypothesis at different levels of significance \(\alpha\).
Fundamentally, a statistical hypothesis is a testable statement about a population parameter that can be evaluated using observed data. To summarize the process of testing a significance of our discovery for proportions, we perform the hypothesis testing following the 5-step process.

Step 1: Formulate the Null Hypothesis (\(H_0\)), which we assume to be true unless there is sufficient evidence to the contrary. Then, alternative Hypothesis (\(H_1\)): test against the null, e.g., \(H_0: p_e - p_c = 0\), and \(H_1: p_e - p_c > 0\). If there is evidence that \(H_0\) is false, we reject \(H_0\) in favor of \(H_1\).
Step 2: Select the significance level \(\alpha\). While \(\alpha = 0.05\) (the 5% level) is the most commonly used, \(\alpha = 0.01\) (the 1% level) is also common.
Step 3: Compute the Test Statistic (\(Z\) or \(T\))
Step 4: Formulate the Decision Rule. For example, reject the Null hypothesis if \(|Z| > 1.96\) (two-sided) or \(Z > 1.64\) (one-sided, upper tail)
Step 5: Make a Decision, Compute the \(p\)-value. \(p\)-value is the smallest significance level at which a null hypothesis can be rejected. If \(p\)-value \(<\alpha\), we reject \(H_0\) and claim we have a discovery. If \(p\)-value is \(\ge \alpha\), then we cannot reject the null-hypothesis.

In Steps 1-2 we formulate the hypothesis. In steps 3-5 we make a decision.
In the context of hypothesis testing, we come back to the type I and type II errors we already discussed. They can be used to describe two types of errors you can make when testing



Error Type
Description




Type I Error
Rejecting a true \(H_0\)


Type II Error
Not rejecting a false \(H_0\)



And the significance level is then \[
P(\mbox{reject } H_0 \mid H_0 \; \mbox{ true}) =
P(\mbox{type I error}).
\]
Hypothesis testing is often used in scientific reporting. For example, the discovery of Higgs Boson was announced as a result of hypothesis testing. Scientists used the five-sigma concept to test the Higgs-Boson hypothesis. This concept, however, is somewhat counter-intuitive. If the particle doesn’t exist, one in 3.5 million is the chance an experiment just like the one announced would nevertheless come up with a result appearing to confirm it does exist. So a \(Z\)-score of five corresponds to a one-sided \(p\)-value of one in 3.5 million (ATLAS Collaboration 2012; CMS Collaboration 2012).
The test statistic (\(T\) or \(Z\)) quantifies uncertainty between the null-hypothesis value and the observed one and is equal to the number of standard deviations they are apart from each other. This value is called the \(Z\)-score, and is calculated as \[
Z = \frac{ \bar{x} - \mu_0 }{s/\sqrt{n}},
\] where \(\mu_0\) is the mean assumed under null-hypothesis. The square root of the statistic’s variance \(s/\sqrt{n}\) is called standard error and is denoted by \(s_{\bar X}\).
Let’s calculate the \(Z\)-score for the yawning example. Let \(\mu_0 = 0\), \(\hat d = \hat p_e - \hat p_c = 0.044\), \(\Var{\hat d}=\Var{\hat p_e - \hat p_c} = 0.0177\), we get \(Z\) statistic to be 0.33 (derived in Example 5.9). Thus, our observed difference is very close to 0.
To summarize the duality of confidence interval, \(p\)-value and \(Z\)-score, the following statements are equivalent (for a two-sided test, with the same standard error throughout):







Statement
Condition




0 is inside the 95% confidence interval
two-sided \(p\)-value is greater than 0.05


two-sided \(p\)-value is greater than 0.05
\(\lvert Z\rvert\) is less than 1.96


\(\lvert Z\rvert\) is less than 1.96
0 is inside the 95% confidence interval




Example 5.3 (Stock Market Crash 1987 (Z-score)) Prior to the October, 1987 crash, SP500 monthly returns were 1.2% with a risk/volatility of 4.3%. The question is how extreme was the 1987 crash of \(-21.76\)%? \[
X \sim N \left(1.2, 4.3^2 \right )
\] This probability distribution can be standardized to yield \[
Z =\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma} = \frac{X - 1.2}{4.3} \sim N(0,1) .
\] Now, we calculate the observed \(Z\), given the outcome of the crash event \[
Z = \frac{-21.76 - 1.2}{4.3} = -5.34
\] That is a \(5\)-sigma event in terms of the distribution of \(X\). Meaning that -21.76 is 5 standard deviations away from the mean. Under a normal model that is equivalent to \(P(X < -21.76) = 4.6593\times 10^{-8}\).



Other Applications

Example 5.4 (Coke vs Pepsi) A classic hypothesis test is whether people can tell the difference between Coke and Pepsi. We run a double blind experiment, neither the experimenter or subject know the allocation. Pepsi claimed that more than half of Diet Coke drinkers said they preferred to drink Diet Pepsi. That is our alternative hypothesis. The data come from a random sample of \(100\) drinkers. We find that \(56\) favor Pepsi.
This is a hypothesis test about the proportion of drinkers who prefer Pepsi \[H_0 : p = \frac{1}{2} \; \; \mathrm{ and} \; \; H_1 : p > \frac{1}{2}\] Let’s estimate our statistics from data: \[\hat{p} = X/n = 56/100 = 0.56\]
This is our best estimate of the true \(p\). The standard error of our statistic \[s_{\hat p} =  \sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})/n} = 0.0496 .\]
The \(95\)% confidence interval is then \[0.56 \pm 1.96 (0.0496) = 0.56 \pm 0.097 = ( 0.463, 0.657 )\] \(p=0.5\) lies inside the confidence interval, so we cannot reject \(H_0\): the data do not give significant evidence for Pepsi’s claim.
The \(Z\)-score now with the null standard error \(\sqrt{ p_0(1-p_0)/n} = 0.05\) \[Z = \frac{ \hat{p} - p_0 }{ \sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}} = \frac{ 0.56-0.5}{0.05} = 1.2 < 1.64\] Let’s take the usual \(\alpha = 0.05\).

prop.test(56, 100, alternative = "greater", conf.level = 0.95) %>% fmt_prop_test()

Don’t reject \(H_0\) for a one-sided test at \(5\)% level (prop.test \(p\)-value with continuity correction: 0.14; the uncorrected \(Z=1.2\) gives 0.115). We need a larger \(n\) to come to a more definitive conclusion. One of the downsides of hypothesis testing is that it generates a yes/no answer without having any uncertainty associated with it.


Example 5.5 (Avonex) Biogen made the following assertion: “Avonex delivers the highest rate of satisfaction: 95% among patients” In response to that statement, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on October 30th, 2002, informed the biotech company Biogen to stop publishing misleading promotions for its multiple sclerosis drug Avonex. To clarify the issue, suppose a random sample of \(75\) patients is surveyed and only 60% say they are satisfied with Avonex (an illustrative survey). The question is: Who is right?
Let’s use hypothesis testing to get an answer. Following our five-step process, we set up the Hypothesis Test:

Formulate the Null Hypothesis: \(H_0 : p = 0.95 = p_0\). The alternative hypothesis: \(H_1 : p < 0.95\). A 1-sided alternative.
We’ll use a small significance level, 1%.
The appropriate test statistic is \(Z = -14\).

To complete our analysis, we need to determine the critical region and calculate the \(p\)-value for this test. For a one-sided test at the 1% significance level, the critical region is \(Z < -2.32\). Since our observed test statistic of \(Z = -14\) falls well within this rejection region, we reject the null hypothesis.
This procedure can be implemented in R in the prop.test function.

prop.test(45, 75, 0.95, alternative = "less") %>% fmt_prop_test()

The \(p\)-value is less than \(2.2 \times 10^{-16}\), which is essentially zero. This extremely small \(p\)-value provides overwhelming statistical evidence against Biogen’s 95% claim.


Example 5.6 (Pfizer) Pfizer introduced Viagra in early 1998. During \(1998\), of the \(6\) million Viagra users, \(77\) died from coronary problems such as heart attacks. Pfizer claimed that this rate is no more than the general population. Suppose that, among \(1{,}500{,}000\) comparable men who were not on Viagra, \(11\) died of coronary problems during the same length of time as the \(77\) Viagra users who died in \(1998\) (illustrative numbers, the comparison is observational). The question is whether the drug is safe. Let’s calculate the confidence interval. A 95% confidence interval for a difference in proportions \(p_1 - p_2\) is \[
( \hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 ) \pm 1.96
\sqrt{ \frac{ \hat{p}_1 ( 1 - \hat{p}_1 ) }{ n_1 }  +
    \frac{ \hat{p}_2 ( 1 - \hat{p}_2 ) }{ n_2 } }
\]
We can do a confidence interval or a \(Z\)-score test. With Viagra, \(\hat{p}_1 = 77/6000000 = 0.00001283\) and without Viagra \(\hat{p}_2 = 11/1500000 = 0.00000733\). We need to test whether these are equal. With a \(95\)% confidence interval for \((p_1 - p_2)\) you get an interval \(( 0.0000003 , 0.0000107).\)
Since this confidence interval does not contain zero, we have evidence that the proportion of deaths from coronary problems is significantly higher among Viagra users compared to the general population. Despite the small proportions involved, the standard errors are small due to the large sample sizes in both groups, but the comparison is observational and the groups are not adjusted for age or other differences. For hypothesis testing, we would use a one-sided test with a significance level of \(\alpha = 0.01\) to test whether the proportion of deaths is higher in the Viagra group. The difference in proportions can be analyzed as follows:

These two conclusions are not contradictory: the evidence is borderline, significant at the 5% two-sided level of the interval but not at the stricter 1% one-sided level of the test.


Example 5.7 (Lord Rayleigh’s Argon Discovery) Lord Rayleigh won the Nobel Prize for discovery of Argon. This discovery occurred when he noticed a small discrepancy between two sets of measurements on nitrogen gas that he had extracted from the air and one he had made in the lab.
First, he removed all oxygen from a sample of air. He measured the density of the remaining gas in a fixed volume at constant temperature and pressure. title: 5  A/B Testing
text:
5.3 A/B Testing Applications

Example 5.8 (SimCity) In the gaming industry, A/B testing is central to optimizing revenue. Electronic Arts is a company that makes video games. SimCity 5, one of EA’s most popular video games, sold 1.1 million copies in the first two weeks of its launch. 50% of sales were digital downloads.
As EA prepared to release the new version of SimCity, they released a promotional offer to drive more game pre-orders. The offer was displayed as a banner across the top of the pre-order page, front and center for shoppers. But according to the team, the promotion was not driving the increase in pre-orders they had expected.
They decided to test some other options to see what design or layout would drive more revenue.








Original







Variation






Figure 5.2: SimCity banner



One variation removed the promotional offer from the page altogether. The test led to some very surprising results: The variation with no offer messaging whatsoever drove 43.4% more purchases. Data revealed that customers preferred a direct purchase path, indicating that additional incentives were unnecessary.
Most people believe that direct promotions drive purchases, but for EA, this turned out not to be true in this test. Testing gave them the information needed to maximize revenue in a way that would not have been otherwise possible.
As a hypothetical follow-up (the numbers are invented for illustration), we define the abtestfunc function to examine whether a black or pink background results in more purchases. Run the experiment for one week:

Pink background: \(40\)% purchase rate with \(500\) visitors
Black background: \(30\)% purchase rate with \(550\) visitors

Let’s run the AB test to see which is more effective. The question is about the difference of the two purchase rates, so the abtestfunc function below computes that difference, its 95% confidence interval with the standard error \(\sqrt{\hat p_1(1-\hat p_1)/n_1 + \hat p_2(1-\hat p_2)/n_2}\), and the two-proportion \(z\) statistic, which uses the pooled rate \(\hat p\) of both groups under the null hypothesis of equal rates.

site1 <- c(.40, 500) # pink
site2 <- c(.30, 550) # black
abtestfunc <- function(ad1, ad2) {
  d <- ad1[1] - ad2[1]
  se <- sqrt(ad1[1] * (1 - ad1[1]) / ad1[2] + ad2[1] * (1 - ad2[1]) / ad2[2])
  p <- (ad1[1] * ad1[2] + ad2[1] * ad2[2]) / (ad1[2] + ad2[2])
  z <- d / sqrt(p * (1 - p) * (1 / ad1[2] + 1 / ad2[2]))
  round(c(diff = d, lower = d - 1.96 * se, upper = d + 1.96 * se, z = z), 3)
}
abtestfunc(site1, site2)
##  diff lower upper     z 
## 0.100 0.042 0.158 3.398

The pink background sells to 10 more visitors in 100, with a 95% confidence interval of 4.2 to 15.8 points, and \(z = 3.40\) (two-sided \(p\)-value 0.0007), so the purchase rate of the pink background is significantly higher. A common shortcut compares the two separate intervals, here the 80% intervals [37, 43] for pink and [28, 32] for black, and calls the difference significant when they do not overlap. That is not a test of the difference: two intervals can overlap while the difference is significant, and the level of the separate intervals says nothing about the level of the comparison.


Example 5.9 (Mythbusters) We now return to the Mythbusters yawning experiment to analyze it using the standard error of the difference in proportions.
The question is what happens if we are to re-run this experiment several times with different groups of participants, will we see the same difference of 4.4%? The fact is that from one experiment to another calculated proportions of yawners in both groups will be different.
In our example, the proportion of yawners in the experimental group is \(\hat p_e = 0.294\) and in the control group is \(\hat p_c = 0.25\). Thus, \[
\hat \sigma^2_e = 0.294(1-0.294) = 0.208,~~~\hat \sigma^2_c = 0.25(1-0.25) = 0.188
\]
We can apply CLT to describe the uncertainty about \(\hat p_{e}\) and \(\hat p_{c}\) \[
\hat p_e\overset{\cdot}{\sim} N(p_e, 0.208/34),~~~ \hat p_c\overset{\cdot}{\sim} N(p_c, 0.188/16),
\] and replace \(p_e\) and \(p_c\) by their estimates 0.294 and 0.25 to plot the estimated sampling distributions. Now, instead of comparing proportions (numbers), we can compare their distributions and thus quantify uncertainties. If we plot density functions of those two Normal variables, we can see that although means are different, there is a large overlap of the two density functions.

p <- seq(0.0, 0.6, length.out = 200)
plot(p, dnorm(p, 0.25, sqrt(0.188 / 16)), col = 2, type = "l", lwd = 3, ylab = "Density", ylim = c(0, 5))
lines(p, dnorm(p, 0.294, sqrt(0.208 / 34)), col = 3, lwd = 3, lty = 2)
legend("topright", c("control", "experiment"), col = c(2, 3), lwd = 3, lty = c(1, 2), bty = "n")








The amount of overlap is the measure of how certain we are that \(p_e\) and \(p_c\) are different. Large overlap means we are not very certain if proportions are truly different. For example, both \(p_e\) and \(p_c\) have a high probability of being between 0.2 and 0.4. We can use properties of normal distribution to say specifically what is the amount of this overlap by calculating the corresponding 95% confidence interval of the difference between the proportions. Note that the difference of two Normal random variables is another Normal \[
\hat p_e - \hat p_c \overset{\cdot}{\sim} N(p_e - p_c, 0.208/34 + 0.188/16) = N(p_e - p_c, 0.0177)
\] Now we can calculate the 95% confidence interval for \(p_e - p_c\) centered at the estimate 0.044, again using properties of Normal

0.044 + c(-1.96, 1.96) * sqrt(0.0177)
## -0.22  0.30

The interval is wide and most importantly, it does contain 0. Thus, we cannot say for sure that the proportions are different. They might just appear to be different due to chance (sampling error). The data are consistent with any true difference between -0.22 and 0.30.
Thus, statistical analysis does not confirm the conclusion made by the show hosts and indicates that there is little evidence that the proportion of yawners is different between the control and experimental groups.


Example 5.10 (Search Algorithm) For tech giants, even small improvements in metrics can lead to massive gains. Let’s look at another (hypothetical) example and test effectiveness of Google’s new search algorithm. We measure effectiveness by the number of users who clicked on one of the search results. As users send the search requests, they will be randomly processed with Algo 1 or Algo 2. We wait until 2500 search requests were processed by each of the algorithms and calculate the following table based on how often people clicked through

p1 <- 1755 / 2500

The intervals slightly overlap, but as Example 5.8 showed, the overlap of two separate intervals is not a test of the difference. The right tool is a confidence interval for the difference of the proportions. Since \(\hat p_1\) and \(\hat p_2\) are approximately normal, so is their difference \[
\hat p_1 - \hat p_2 \overset{\cdot}{\sim} N(p_1 - p_2, s_1^2/n + s_2^2/n), \quad s_i^2 = \hat p_i(1-\hat p_i).

The confidence interval for the difference is (-0.054, -0.004), which does not contain 0, and thus we can say that we are confident that algorithms are different!
More generally, if the number of observations in two groups are different, say \(n_1\) and \(n_2\) then the \[

title: 5  A/B Testing
text:
5.4 Challenges in A/B Testing

Multiple Testing
Consider this simple multiple-testing scenario. If we want to test 1000 hypotheses and we test each hypothesis one-by-one, say the ground truth is that only 10% (100) of those hypotheses have a real effect (the null is false). Using \(\alpha=0.05\) rule, we assume that out of 900 true nulls \(0.05 \cdot 900 = 45\) will show up as positive (false positives). Now we run our one-by-one hypothesis tests (with power 0.8), and our procedure correctly identified 80 out of 100 true positives and incorrectly identified 45 false positives and 20 false negatives. Now, among 125 hypotheses identified as positives, 45 in fact are not! Another way to look at it is to calculate the probability of at least one false positive \(P(\mbox{at least one false positive}) = 1 - (1-0.05)^{1000} \approx 1\) for independent tests when all nulls are true. We are almost guaranteed to see at least one false positive.








Figure 5.3: Probability of At Least 1 False Positive.





One way to deal with the problem is to lower the cut-off to \(\alpha/m\). This approach is called the Bonferroni correction. For the case of 1000 hypotheses, we set \(\alpha = 0.00005\). However, this conservative approach will lead to many false negatives. If all 1000 null hypotheses are true and the tests are independent, the probability of at least one false positive is then \(1 - (1-0.00005)^{1000} = 0.049\).

Classification of results for a testing procedure. T/F = True/False, D/N = Discovery/Non-discovery. We observe \(m\), \(D\) and \(N\).

A more practical approach is to use the False Discovery Rate \[
\text{FDR} = \E{\frac{FD}{\max(D,1)}}
\] which is the expected proportion of false positives among all significant results. We aim to set a cutoff so that FDR \(\le Q\). The FDR approach allows us to increase the power while maintaining some principled bound on error.
Benjamini and Hochberg developed a procedure based on FDR to perform multiple testing (Benjamini and Hochberg 1995). Under their procedure, we put individual \(p\)-values in order from smallest to largest. Then we choose the largest \(p_k\) value that is at most \((k/m)Q\) where \(Q\) is the false discovery rate you choose. Then all hypotheses with index \(i \le k\) are significant. Benjamini and Hochberg showed that under this procedure the FDR \(\le Q\) when the tests are independent, and Benjamini and Yekutieli later showed that it also holds under positive dependence (Benjamini and Yekutieli 2001).
As an example, García-Arenzana et al. (2014) tested associations of 25 dietary variables with mammographic density, an important risk factor for breast cancer, in Spanish women. Ordered by \(p\)-value, the first seven of their 25 tests are shown below with the Benjamini–Hochberg critical value \((k/25)Q\) for \(Q = 0.25\).
