  1.2, 0,
  0, -0.2
), ncol = 2)
Q <- 0.3 * Sigma
K <- A %*% Sigma %*% t(G) %*% solve(G %*% Sigma %*% t(G) + R)
xhatnew <- A %*% xhat + K %*% (y - G %*% xhat)
Sigmanew <- A %*% Sigma %*% t(A) - K %*% G %*% Sigma %*% t(A) + Q











Forward filtering and Backwards Sampling
The Kalman filtering recursions lead to a fully recursive algorithm for characterizing \(p( x \mid y)\) known as FFBS (Forward filtering and Backwards Sampling). This provides the counterpart to the forward-backward recursions for HMMs in the next section. The details are as follows. The first step is to factorize the joint posterior distribution of the states via \[\begin{align*}
p\left(  x \mid y^{T}\right)   &  =p\left(  x_{T} \mid y^{T}\right)  \prod_{t=1}%
^{T-1}p\left(  x_{t} \mid x_{t+1},...,x_{T},y^{T}\right)  \\
&  =p\left(  x_{T} \mid y^{T}\right)  \prod_{t=1}^{T-1}p\left(  x_{t} \mid x_{t+1}%
,y^{t}\right)
\end{align*}\] where we have used the fact that \(p\left(  x_{t} \mid x_{t+1},...,x_{T},y^{T}\right)  =p\left(  x_{t} \mid x_{t+1},y^{t}\right)\) by the Markov property. Conditioning on \(x_{t+1}\) removes two things at once: the later states \(x_{t+2},\ldots,x_{T}\), and the later observations \(y_{t+1},\ldots,y_{T}\), since in a state space model each \(y_{s}\) for \(s>t\) depends on the past only through \(x_{t+1}\). This is why the conditioning set collapses from \(y^{T}\) all the way down to \(y^{t}\), which is what makes the backward pass usable: every ingredient is already available from the forward filter.
This forms the FFBS algorithm: forward-filtering, backward sampling algorithm for generating a block sample from \(p\left(  x \mid y^{T}\right)\). Filter forward using the Kalman recursions and obtain a sample from \(p( x_T \mid y^T)\) and then backwards sample using \(p\left(x_{t} \mid x_{t+1},y^{t}\right)\) to generate a block draw of \(x\). In what follows, we will often write \[
p\left(  x \mid y^{T}\right)  \sim FFBS
\] to denote that the FFBS algorithm can be used to generate a block draw.
Backwards Sampling.
The distribution of the final state given the data history \(p( x_{T} \mid y^{T} )\) is given by the Kalman filter \[
p( x_{T} \mid y^{T}) \sim\mathcal{N}\left(  \mu_{T},\Sigma_{T}\right)
\] where \(( \mu_{T} , \Sigma_{T} )\) are computed via the Kalman filter recursions. The second distribution comes from the factorization of \(p( x_{t}, x_{t+1} \mid y^{t} )\) in the derivation of the Kalman filtering recursions. Hence, the conditional state filtering distribution given \(( x_{t+1} , y^t )\) is \[
p( x_{t} \mid x_{t+1} , y^{t} ) \sim\mathcal{N}\left(  \mu_{t\mid t+1} ,
\Sigma_{t\mid t+1} \right)
\] where the one-step back smoothed moments are \[\begin{align*}
\mu_{t\mid t+1}  &  = \Sigma_{t\mid t+1} \left(  \Sigma_{t\mid t}^{-1} \mu_{t\mid t} +
G_{t+1}^\top\left(  \Sigma^{x}_{t+1} \right)  ^{-1} x_{t+1} \right) \\
\Sigma_{t\mid t+1}^{-1}  &  = G_{t+1}^\top\left(  \Sigma^{x}_{t+1} \right)  ^{-1}
G_{t+1} + \Sigma_{t\mid t}^{-1}%
\end{align*}\] as computed above. Then we can sequentially sample from this distribution.


HMM: Hidden Markov Models
The forward and backward recursions of this section go back to Baum et al. (1970), and the related decoding algorithm to Viterbi (1967). Baum developed original trading algorithms for Renaissance Technologies which later became a multi-billion-dollar hedge fund. The algorithms are also known as the Baum-Welch and Viterbi algorithms, respectively. Baum-Welch estimates the parameters of a Hidden Markov Model (HMM) from a sequence of observations. The HMM is a statistical model that describes a system that is assumed to be a Markov process with unobserved (hidden) states. These algorithms are now widely used in many applications, including speech recognition, bioinformatics, and finance.
Viterbi, on the other hand, was one of the founders of what is now known as Qualcomm, a multi-billion-dollar semiconductor and telecommunications equipment company. Viterbi’s algorithm is used to find the most likely sequence of hidden states in a Hidden Markov Model (HMM) given a sequence of observations.
Consider a model with a Hidden Chain or regime-switching variable
\[
y_{t} = \mu\left( x_{t}\right) + \sigma\left( x_{t}\right) \varepsilon _{t}\text{.}
\]
Suppose that \(x_{t}\) is a finite-state Markov chain with a time-homogeneous transition matrix \(P\) with entries \(\left\{ p_{ij}\right\}\) which are given by
\[
p_{ij} = P\left( x_{t} = j \mid x_{t-1} = i, \theta\right) \text{.}
\]
We define the marginal filtering and smoothing distributions
\[
p_{i}^{t,t} = P\left( x_{t} = i \mid \theta, y^{t}\right) \text{ and } p_{i}^{t,T} = P\left( x_{t} = i \mid \theta, y^{T}\right)
\]
and the corresponding joint filtering and smoothing matrices:
\[
p_{ij}^{t,t} = P\left( x_{t-1} = i, x_{t} = j \mid \theta, y^{t}\right) \text{ and } p_{ij}^{t,T} = P\left( x_{t-1} = i, x_{t} = j \mid \theta, y^{T}\right) \text{.}
\]
The key to the algorithm is that we are just going to track the joint matrices, and then peel-off marginals from the rows and columns.

Forward-filtering
To derive the forward equations
\[
\begin{aligned}
p_{ij}^{t,t} & = P\left( x_{t-1} = i, x_{t} = j \mid \theta, y^{t}\right) \propto p\left( y_{t}, x_{t-1} = i, x_{t} = j \mid \theta, y^{t-1}\right) \\
& \propto p\left( y_{t} \mid x_{t} = j, \theta\right) p\left( x_{t} = j \mid x_{t-1} = i, \theta\right) p\left( x_{t-1} = i \mid \theta, y^{t-1}\right) \\
& \propto p\left( y_{t} \mid x_{t} = j, \theta\right) p_{ij}\left( p_{i}^{t-1,t-1}\right) \text{.}
\end{aligned}
\]
This shows how to compute today’s filtering distribution given the likelihood. The advantage of this is that it only requires matrix multiplication.


Backward smoothing
The result of the forward-filtering is the final observation \(p_{ij}^{T,T}\). Like in the previous section, we can then filter in reverse to compute \(p_{ij}^{t,T}\), which is required for the MCMC algorithm. We have that
\[
\begin{aligned}
p_{ij}^{t,T} & = p\left( x_{t-1} = i, x_{t} = j \mid \theta, y^{T}\right) \\
& \propto p\left( x_{t-1} = i \mid x_{t} = j, \theta, y^{T}\right) p\left( x_{t} = j \mid \theta, y^{T}\right) \\
& \propto p\left( x_{t-1} = i \mid x_{t} = j, \theta, y^{t}\right) p\left( x_{t} = j \mid \theta, y^{T}\right) \\
& \propto \frac{p\left( x_{t-1} = i, x_{t} = j \mid \theta, y^{t}\right)}{p\left( x_{t} = j \mid \theta, y^{t}\right)} p\left( x_{t} = j \mid \theta, y^{T}\right) \\
& \propto p_{ij}^{t,t} \frac{p_{j}^{t,T}}{p_{j}^{t,t}} \text{.}
\end{aligned}
\]
In deriving this, we have used the fact that
\[
p\left( x_{t-1} = i \mid x_{t} = j, \theta, y^{T}\right) \propto p\left( x_{t-1} = i \mid x_{t} = j, \theta , y^{t}\right)
\]
because conditional on time \(t\) information, the past transition is independent of the future. Sampling from these probabilities instead gives the discrete-state version of the FFBS algorithm.


Smoothing: Forwards and Backwards
Let \(y^T = \{y_1, \dots, y_T\}\) be a sequence of random variables where the conditional distribution
\[
p(y^T \mid x^T) = p (y_1 \mid x_1 ) \prod_{t=2}^T p(y_t \mid x_t, y_{t-1})
\]
where we suppress the dependence of the mixture components on a parameter \(\theta\). The full smoothing distribution can be written
\[
p( x \mid y ) = p( x_T \mid y^T ) \prod_{t=1}^{T-1} p( x_t \mid x_{t+1} , \theta , y^{t} )
\]
Suppose \(\{x_t\}\) follows a finite-state Markov chain with initial distribution \(\pi_0\) and transition probabilities
\[
Q_t(r,s) = Pr(x_t = s \mid x_{t-1} = r) \; \; \mathrm{and} \; \; P_t ( t, r ,s) = Pr(x_{t-1} = r, x_t = s \mid y_1^t)
\]
which we will compute sequentially. Let the current filtering distribution of the state be given by, for \(t > 0\),
\[
p_t(s) = Pr(x_t = s \mid y^t) \; \; \mathrm{and} \; \; A_t(x_{t-1}, x_t, y_t) = p(x_{t-1}, x_t, y_t \mid y^{t-1})
\]
By definition,
\[
A_t(r,s,y_t) = p_{t-1}(r) Q_t(r,s) p(y_t \mid x_t = s, y_{t-1}),
\tag{15.1}\]
and the marginal likelihood is given by
\[
p(y_t \mid y_{1}^{t-1}) = \sum_{r,s} A_t(r,s,y_t)
\]
The filtered transition distribution
\[
p_{trs} = A_t(r,s,y_t) / p(y_t \mid y^{t-1})
\]
The forward-backward recursions are used to efficiently compute the observed data likelihood
\[
p(y) = \sum_{ x } p(y \mid x)p( x )
\]
where \(x = ( x_1 , \ldots , x_T )\). We also need the posterior distribution \(p( x \mid y )\) of the latent Markov chain given observed data. The recursions consist of a forward step that computes the distribution of the \(t\)’th transition given all the data up to time \(t\), and a backward recursion that updates each distribution to condition on all observed data.
The forward recursion operates on the set of transition distributions, represented by a sequence of matrices \(P_t = ( p_{trs} )\). Computing
\[
p_t(s) = \sum_{r}p_{trs}
\]
sets up the next step in the recursion. The recursion is initialized by replacing \(p_{t-1}\) with \(\pi_0\) in equation Equation 15.1.
The observed data log-likelihood can be computed as
\[
\log p(y) = \log p(y_1) + \sum_{t=2}^T \log p(y_t \mid y^{t-1})
\]
With appropriate use of logarithms, \(p\) and \(p(y_t \mid y^{t-1})\) need only ever be evaluated on the log scale.
The stochastic version of the backward recursion simulates from
\[
p(x \mid y).
\]
Begin with the factorization
\[
p(x \mid y) = p(x_T \mid y^T) \prod_{t=1}^{T-1} p(x_{t} \mid x_{t+1}^T, y).
\]
Then notice that, given \(x_{t+1}\), \(x_t\) is conditionally independent of \(y_{t+1}^T\) and all later \(x\)’s. Thus
\[
p(x_t \mid x_{t+1}, y) = P(x_t = r \mid x_{t+1} = s, y^{t+1}) \propto p_{t+1rs}
\]
Therefore, if one samples \((x_{T-1}, x_T)\) from the discrete bivariate distribution given by \(P_T\) and then repeatedly samples \(x_t\) from a multinomial distribution proportional to column \(x_{t+1}\) of \(P_{t+1}\) then \(x=(x_1, \ldots , x_T)\) is a draw from \(p(x \mid y)\).



Mixture Kalman Filter
We can also introduce a \(\lambda_t\) state variable and consider a system
\[
\begin{aligned}
y_t & = F_{\lambda_t} x_t + D_{\lambda_t} \epsilon_t  \\
x_t & = G_{\lambda_t} x_{t-1} + B_{\lambda_t} v_t
\end{aligned}
\]
The Kalman filter gives moments of the state filtering distribution
\[
x_t \mid \lambda^t , y^t \sim \mathcal{N} \left ( \mu_{t\mid t} , \Sigma_{t\mid t} \right )
\]
Here we assume that the i.i.d. auxiliary state variable shocks \(\lambda_t \sim p( \lambda_t )\).
First we marginalize over the state variable \(x_t\). Then we can track the sufficient statistics of the filtering distribution of \(x_t\) dynamically in time, namely \(\left ( \mu_{t\mid t} , \Sigma_{t\mid t} \right )\), just the Kalman filter moments, in the conditionally Gaussian and discrete cases Lindgren (1978).


Regime Switching Models
The general form of a continuous-time regime switching model is
\[
dy_{t}=\mu\left(  \theta,x_{t},y_{t}\right)  dt+\sigma\left(  \theta
,x_{t},y_{t}\right)  d B_{t}%
\]
where \(x_{t}\) takes values in a discrete space with transition matrix \(P_{ij}\left(  t\right)\) with parameters \(\theta=\left(  \theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{J}\right)\). Common specifications assume the drift and diffusion coefficients are parametric functions and the parameters switch over time. In this case, it is common to write the model as
\[
dy_{t}=\mu\left(  \theta_{x_{t}},y_{t}\right)  dt+\sigma\left(  \theta_{x_{t}%
},y_{t}\right)  d B_{t}\text{.}%
\]
Steven L. Scott (2002) provides a fast MCMC algorithm for state filtering by adapting the FFBS algorithm. Time-discretized, the model is:
\[
y_{t}=\mu\left(  \theta_{x_{t}},y_{t-1}\right)  +\sigma\left(  \theta_{x_{t}%
},y_{t-1}\right)  \varepsilon_{t}\text{.}%
\]
Note that we use the standard notation from discrete-time models where the time index on the Markov state is equal to the current observation. The discrete-time transition probabilities are
\[
p_{ij}=P\left(  x_{t}=j \mid x_{t-1}=i\right)
\]
and we assume, a priori, that the transition functions are time invariant. The joint likelihood is given by
\[
p\left(  y \mid x,\theta\right)  = \prod_{t=1}^{T} p\left(  y_{t} \mid y_{t-1}%
,x_{t},\theta\right)\]
where \(p\left(  y_{t} \mid y_{t-1},x_{t},\theta\right)  =N\left(  \mu\left(
\theta_{x_{t}},y_{t-1}\right)  ,\sigma^{2}\left(  \theta_{x_{t}}%
,y_{t-1}\right)  \right)\).
Clifford-Hammersley implies that the complete conditionals are given by \(p\left(  \theta \mid x ,P , y \right)\), \(p\left(  P \mid x , \theta, y \right)\), and \(p\left(  x \mid P ,\theta, y \right)\). Conditional on the states and the transition probabilities, updating the parameters is straightforward. Conditional on the states and under independent Dirichlet priors on its rows, each row of the transition matrix has a Dirichlet distribution, and updating this is also straightforward. To update the states use FFBS.
An important component of regime switching models is the prior distribution. Regime switching models (and most mixture models) are not formally identified. For example, in all regime switching models, there is a labeling problem: there is no unique way to identify the states. A common approach to overcome this identification issue is to order the parameters.

Changepoint Problems
Smith (1975) introduced the single changepoint problem from a Bayesian perspective. Consider a sequence of random variables \(y_{1} , \ldots, y_{T}\) which has a change-point at time \(\tau\) in the sense that
\[
y_t \mid \theta_{k} \sim    \left\{
\begin{array}[c]{l}
p( y \mid \theta_{1} ) \; \; \; \; \; \; \mathrm{for} \; \; 1 \leq t \leq\tau \\
p( y \mid \theta_{2} ) \; \; \; \; \; \; \mathrm{for} \; \; \tau+1 \leq
t \leq T
\end{array}  \right\}\]
This can be rewritten as a state space model
\[
y_t = \theta_{ x_t } + \sigma_{ x_t } \epsilon_t
\]
where \(x_t\) has a Markov transition evolution.
An idea that appears to be under-exploited is that of “model reparametrisation”. The multiple change-point problem, which is computationally expensive if approached directly, has a natural model reparametrisation that makes the implementation of MCMC methods straightforward (see Chib (1998)). Specifically, suppose that the data generating process \(y^{T} = \{ y_{1} , \ldots, y_{T} \}\) is given by a sequence of conditionals \(f ( y_{t} \mid y^{t-1} , \theta_{k} )\) for parameters \(\theta_{k}\) that change at unknown change-points \(\{ \tau_{1} , \ldots,
\tau_{k} \}\).
The model parameterization is based on using a hidden Markov state space model with a vector of latent variables \(x_{t}\) where \(x_{t}
= k\) indicates that \(y_{t}\) is drawn from \(p ( y_{t} \mid y^{t-1} ,
\theta_{k} )\). Let the prior distribution on the \(x_{t}\)’s have a transition matrix where \(p_{ij} = P \left(  x_{t} = j \mid x_{t-1} = i
\right)\) is the probability of jumping regimes, with \(x_1 = 1\) and \(p_{ij} = 0\) unless \(j \in \{i, i+1\}\), so the chain either stays in its regime or moves to the next. With this model parameterization, the \(k\)th change occurs at \(\tau_{k}\) if \(x_{
\tau_{k} } = k\) and \(x_{ \tau_{k} + 1 } = k + 1\). The reparameterisation automatically enforces the order constraints on the change-points, and it is very easy to perform MCMC analysis on the posterior distribution. This provides a more efficient strategy for posterior computation. MCMC analysis of the \(x_{t}\)’s is straightforward, and the posterior for the \(\tau_{k}\)’s can be obtained by inverting the definition above. Hence
\[
p( \tau_k = t \mid y ) = p( x_t = k, x_{t+1} = k + 1 \mid y )
\]
The alternative is single-state updating conditional on \(\tau\) which is slow for finding the multiple change points.

title: 15  Forecasting
section: 15.12 Particle Learning for General Mixture Models
text:
15.12 Particle Learning for General Mixture Models
Particle learning (PL) offers a powerful and flexible approach for sequential inference in general mixture models. Unlike traditional MCMC methods, which require repeated passes over the entire dataset and can be computationally demanding, particle learning operates in an online fashion. This means it can efficiently update inference as new data arrive, making it particularly well-suited for large or high-dimensional datasets and real-time applications.
The particle learning framework is designed to efficiently and sequentially learn from a broad class of mixture models. At its core, the approach models data as arising from a mixture distribution:
\[
f(z) = \int k(z;\theta) d G(\theta)
\]
where \(G\) is a discrete mixing measure and \(k(z;\theta)\) is a kernel parameterized by \(\theta\). The generality of this formulation allows PL to be applied to a wide variety of models, including finite mixture models, Dirichlet process mixtures, Indian buffet processes, and probit stick-breaking models.
In addition to its generality, particle learning provides an alternative to MCMC for tasks such as online model fitting, marginal likelihood estimation, and posterior cluster allocation.
A general mixture model can be described by three components: a likelihood, a transition equation for latent allocations, and a prior over parameters. Specifically,

The likelihood is given by \(p(y_{t+1} \mid k_{t+1}, \theta)\), representing the probability of the next observation given the current allocation and parameters.
The transition equation \(p(k_{t+1} \mid k^t, \theta)\) governs how the latent allocation variables evolve over time, where \(k^t = \{k_1,\ldots, k_t\}\) denotes the history of allocations.
The parameter prior \(p(\theta)\) encodes prior beliefs about the mixture component parameters.

This structure can be expressed in a state-space form:
\[\begin{align*}
y_{t+1} &= f(k_{t+1}, \theta) \\
k_{t+1} &= g(k^t, \theta)
\end{align*}\]
where the first equation is the observation model and the second describes the evolution of the latent allocation states.
The mixture modeling framework described above is closely related to hidden Markov models (HMMs). In this context, the observed data \(y_t\) are assumed to be generated from a mixture, with allocation variables \(k_t\) determining which mixture component is responsible for each observation. The parameters \(\theta_{k_t}\) for each component are drawn from the mixing measure \(G\). This structure allows for both standard mixture models, where each observation is assigned to a single component, and more general latent feature models, where multivariate allocation variables \(k_t\) allow an observation to be associated with multiple components simultaneously.
A central concept in particle learning is the essential state vector \(\mathcal{Z}_t\), which is tracked over time. This vector is constructed to be sufficient for sequential inference, meaning that it contains all the information needed to compute the posterior predictive distribution for new data, update the state as new observations arrive, and learn about the underlying parameters:

Posterior predictive: \(p(y_{t+1} \mid \mathcal{Z}_t)\)
Posterior updating: \(p(\mathcal{Z}_{t+1} \mid \mathcal{Z}_t, y_{t+1})\)
Parameter learning: \(p(\theta \mid \mathcal{Z}_{t+1})\)


The Particle Learning Algorithm
Particle learning approximates the posterior distribution \(p(\mathcal{Z}_t \mid y^t)\) with a set of equally weighted particles \(\{\mathcal{Z}_t^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N\). When a new observation \(y_{t+1}\) becomes available, the algorithm proceeds in two main steps:

Resample: The current set of particles is resampled with weights proportional to the predictive likelihood \(p(y_{t+1} \mid \mathcal{Z}_t^{(i)})\). This step focuses computational effort on the most plausible states given the new data.
Propagate: Each resampled particle is then propagated forward by sampling from the transition distribution \(p(\mathcal{Z}_{t+1} \mid \mathcal{Z}_t^{(i)}, y_{t+1})\), thus updating the state to incorporate the new observation.

This two-step process is grounded in Bayes’ theorem, where the resampling step corresponds to updating the posterior with the new data, and the propagation step advances the state according to the model dynamics. After these steps, the set of particles provides an updated approximation to the posterior \(p(\mathcal{Z}_{t+1} \mid y^{t+1})\).
One important distinction between particle learning and standard particle filtering methods is that the essential state vector \(\mathcal{Z}_t\) does not necessarily need to include the full history of allocation variables \(k^t\) to be sufficient for inference. This makes PL both more efficient and more flexible than many existing particle filtering approaches for mixture models. Furthermore, the order of resampling and propagation steps is reversed compared to standard filters, which helps mitigate particle degeneracy and improves performance in mixture modeling contexts.
Particle learning also provides an efficient mechanism for sampling from the full posterior distribution of the allocation vector \(p(k^t \mid y^t)\). This is achieved using a backwards uncertainty update, which allows for the recovery of smoothed samples of the allocation history. For each particle, and for each time step in reverse order, the allocation variable \(k_r\) is sampled with probability proportional to the product of the likelihood and the prior for that allocation, given the state vector. This results in an algorithm with computational complexity linear in the number of particles, making it practical even for large datasets.
The particle learning framework is applicable to a wide range of density estimation problems involving mixtures of the form
\[
f(y;G) = \int k(y ; \theta) dG(\theta)
\]
There are many possible choices for the prior on the mixing measure \(G\). Common examples include finite mixture models, which use a finite number of components; Dirichlet process mixtures, which allow for an infinite number of components via a stick-breaking construction; beta two-parameter processes; and kernel stick-breaking processes.
In some cases, it is useful to consider a collapsed state-space model, where the predictive distribution for a new observation is expressed as an expectation over the mixing measure \(G\) given the current state vector:
\[
\E{f(y_{t+1};G) \mid \mathcal{Z}_t} = \int k(y_{t+1};\theta) d \E{G(\theta) \mid \mathcal{Z}_t}
\]
If \(t\) observations have been allocated to \(m_t\) mixture components, the posterior expectation of \(G\) can be written as a weighted sum of the base measure and point masses at the component parameters. The predictive density then combines contributions from both new and existing components, weighted according to their posterior probabilities.

Example 15.5 (Particle Learning for Poisson Mixture Models) We will implement Particle Learning (PL) for a finite mixture of Poisson distributions based on the example from Carvalho et al. (2010). This example follows Algorithm 1 for finite mixture models from Section 2.1 of the paper.
We generate data from a mixture of two Poisson distributions (\(\lambda_1=2\) with weight 0.7, \(\lambda_2=10\) with weight 0.3).

set.seed(8) # Ovi
# Simulate data (500 observations)
n_obs <- 500
true_z <- sample(1:2, n_obs, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.7, 0.3))
y <- ifelse(true_z == 1, rpois(n_obs, 2), rpois(n_obs, 10))










The implementation (about 80 lines of R, in code/15-forecasting.R) follows these steps:

Particle Initialization:

Each particle tracks sufficient statistics:

s: Sum of observations per component
n: Count of observations per component


PL Algorithm:

Resample: Particles are weighted by the posterior predictive probability of the next observation
Propagate: For each particle:

Compute component allocation probabilities
Sample component assignment
Update sufficient statistics

Learn: Store posterior estimates of \(\lambda\) parameters and mixture weights


The key features of this implementation are the use of the Poisson-Gamma posterior predictive, a negative binomial distribution, both to weight the particles and to allocate the new observation, and the combination of the prior weights of the components with that predictive probability in the allocation.











(a) Rates.











(b) Weights.







Figure 15.10: Particle Learning for the two-component Poisson mixture: posterior means of the rates and of the weights as the observations arrive. The thin horizontal lines mark the true values.



Figure 15.10 (a) shows the posterior means of the rates \(\lambda\) against the true values (2 and 10), and Figure 15.10 (b) the posterior means of the mixture weights against the true weights (0.7 and 0.3). The two components have the same prior, so the data do not fix their labels, and here the labels are swapped relative to the simulation: component 1 ends near 9.8 with weight near 0.32 and component 2 near 2.2 with weight near 0.68. With the labels matched, the estimates end close to what the simulated sample shows: the sample means of the two groups are 2.0 and 10.0, and their shares of the 500 observations are 0.69 and 0.31. The paths settle after about 450 observations. At the end of the run only 67 distinct states remain among the 1000 particles, the price of multinomial resampling at every observation.
Advantages of PL for Mixtures:

Sequential Updating: Processes observations one-at-a-time
Efficiency: Only tracks sufficient statistics, not full history
Flexibility: Easily extends to other mixture types (DP, IBP, etc.)
Real-time Inference: Posterior updates after each observation

This implementation demonstrates PL’s ability to handle finite mixtures, but the same framework extends to infinite mixtures (DP mixtures) and other general mixture models described in the paper by modifying the propagation and resampling steps.

title: 15  Forecasting
text:
Exercises

Pen-and-Pencil

Exercise 15.1 (State-Space Model Specification) Write out the observation and transition equations for a structural time series model with a local linear trend and quarterly seasonality (\(S=4\)).

Define the state vector \(\alpha_t\) and write the observation equation \(y_t = Z_t^\top \alpha_t + \varepsilon_t\).
Write the transition equations for the level \(\mu_t\), slope \(\delta_t\), and seasonal component \(\tau_t\).
How many state variables does this model have?
If you add a regression component with \(k\) predictors using spike-and-slab priors, how does the model change?



Exercise 15.2 (Kalman Filter Update) The Kalman filter performs Bayesian updating for linear Gaussian state-space models. Consider the simplest case: a random walk plus noise model.
State equation: \(x_{t+1} = x_t + w_t\), where \(w_t \sim N(0, \sigma_w^2)\).
Observation equation: \(y_t = x_t + v_t\), where \(v_t \sim N(0, \sigma_v^2)\).
(Here \(w_t\) is the state noise and \(v_t\) the observation noise, corresponding to the chapter’s \(\eta_t\) and \(\varepsilon_t\).)
Suppose at time \(t\) we have \(x_t \mid y_{1:t} \sim N(\hat{x}_t, P_t)\).

Write the predictive distribution \(x_{t+1} \mid y_{1:t}\).
Write the joint distribution of \((x_{t+1}, y_{t+1})\) given \(y_{1:t}\).
Derive the filtering distribution \(x_{t+1} \mid y_{1:t+1}\) using the normal-normal conjugacy from Chapter 3.
Identify the Kalman gain \(K_{t+1}\) and interpret it. What happens when \(\sigma_v^2 \gg \sigma_w^2\)? When \(\sigma_v^2 \ll \sigma_w^2\)?



Exercise 15.3 (Forward Filtering and Viterbi Decoding for a Two-State HMM) The Kalman filter derived above is the linear-Gaussian filtering recursion. Its discrete-state analogue is the hidden Markov model. Consider a two-state HMM for a volatility regime \(x_t \in \{1, 2\}\), where state 1 is low-volatility and state 2 is high-volatility. The initial distribution is \(\pi = (\prob{x_1 = 1}, \prob{x_1 = 2}) = (0.6, 0.4)\), and the time-homogeneous transition probabilities \(P_{ij} = \prob{x_t = j \mid x_{t-1} = i}\) are
\[
P = \begin{pmatrix} 0.9 & 0.1 \\ 0.2 & 0.8 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
(This is the row-stochastic convention of the chapter, which writes the entries as \(p_{ij}\): each row sums to one.) Each day is observed as calm (C) or turbulent (T), with emission probabilities \(b_j(y) = \prob{y_t = y \mid x_t = j}\) given by \(\prob{y_t = T \mid x_t = 1} = 0.2\) and \(\prob{y_t = T \mid x_t = 2} = 0.7\). You observe \(y_{1:4} = (C, C, T, T)\).

Using the forward recursion, compute by hand the unnormalized forward messages \(\alpha_t(j) = p(y_{1:t}, x_t = j)\) for \(t = 1, \ldots, 4\) and the filtered probabilities \(\prob{x_t = j \mid y_{1:t}}\). Present a \(4 \times 2\) table and report the marginal likelihood \(p(y_{1:4})\).
Compute the Viterbi path maximizing \(p(x_{1:4}, y_{1:4})\): build the \(\delta_t(j)\) table with backpointers \(\psi_t(j)\) and report the decoded state sequence.
Compare \(\arg\max_j \prob{x_4 = j \mid y_{1:4}}\) from (a) with the Viterbi state at \(t = 4\) from (b). Do they agree? Explain why the marginal decoder and the jointly-optimal Viterbi path need not agree in general, even though they do here.
Baum-Welch (Baum et al. 1970) treats \(P\) and the emission probabilities as unknown and re-estimates them by EM. Using \(\gamma_t(j) = \prob{x_t = j \mid y_{1:T}}\) and \(\xi_t(i, j) = \prob{x_{t-1} = i, x_t = j \mid y_{1:T}}\) as the E-step quantities, write the M-step update formulas for \(\hat P_{ij}\), for \(\prob{y_t = T \mid x_t = j}\), and for the initial distribution.



Exercise 15.4 (Local vs. Semilocal Linear Trend) Two trend models are commonly used in structural time series:
Local linear trend: \(\mu_{t+1} = \mu_t + \delta_t + \eta_{0t}\), \(\delta_{t+1} = \delta_t + \eta_{1t}\).
Semilocal linear trend: \(\mu_{t+1} = \mu_t + \delta_t + \eta_{0t}\), \(\delta_{t+1} = D + \rho(\delta_t - D) + \eta_{1t}\), where \(|\rho| < 1\).

In the local linear trend, show that the slope \(\delta_t\) follows a random walk. What does this imply about long-term forecast uncertainty?
In the semilocal model, show that \(\E{\delta_t}\) converges to \(D\) as \(t \to \infty\), regardless of the initial slope.
Which model would you choose for S&P 500 forecasting? For quarterly GDP growth? Justify your answers.



Exercise 15.5 (True/False: Forecasting)  

The Kalman filter assumes that state transitions and observations are linear functions with Gaussian noise.
In a BSTS model with spike-and-slab priors, the expected model size controls how many predictors are included a priori.
A local linear trend model produces forecast intervals that converge to a fixed width as the forecast horizon increases.
The bsts package uses maximum likelihood estimation to fit structural time series models.
Stationarity of a time series means that its mean and variance do not change over time, and the autocovariance \(\Cov{y_t, y_{t+k}}\) depends only on the lag \(k\), not on \(t\).




Computing

Exercise 15.6 (Structural Time Series with bsts) Use the AirPassengers dataset (monthly airline passengers, 1949–1960) to fit structural time series models.

Plot the time series. Does it appear to have a trend? Seasonality? Is the variance constant?
Apply a log transformation and fit a BSTS model with a local linear trend and monthly seasonality (\(S=12\)). Plot the fitted components.
Hold out the last 12 months. Fit the model on the training data and produce 12-month-ahead forecasts. Plot the forecasts with prediction intervals.
Compare the one-step-ahead prediction errors for models with and without the seasonal component using mean absolute one-step-ahead error (MAE).



Exercise 15.7 (Kalman Filter from Scratch) Implement a simple Kalman filter for the random walk plus noise model: \(x_{t+1} = x_t + w_t\), \(y_t = x_t + v_t\).

Generate 100 observations from this model with \(\sigma_w = 1\) and \(\sigma_v = 2\). Plot the true state and noisy observations.
Implement the Kalman filter: prediction step, update step, and Kalman gain. Filter the observations and plot the filtered state alongside the true state.
Plot the Kalman gain \(K_t\) over time. Does it converge? To what value? (Report the iteration at which |K_t - K_{t-1}| first falls below 1e-6.)
Repeat with \(\sigma_v = 0.1\) (precise observations). How does the filtered estimate change?



Exercise 15.8 (Dynamic Logistic State-Space Model for a Binary Series) The recession-modeling example in this chapter fits a dynamic logistic regression with a random-walk level, \(\mathrm{logit}(p_t) = \mu_t + \beta^\top x_t\), \(\mu_{t+1} = \mu_t + \eta_t\), using bsts. Here you simulate a simplified version (no regressors) and filter it yourself: the Bernoulli observation equation means the closed-form Kalman recursions of the previous exercise no longer apply, so a simulation-based filter is needed instead.

Simulate a latent log-odds \(\theta_t\) following a Gaussian random walk for \(T=150\) periods: \(\theta_1 = -1\) and \(\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t + \eta_t\) with \(\eta_t \sim N(0, \sigma_w^2)\), \(\sigma_w = 0.35\). Set \(p_t = \mathrm{logit}^{-1}(\theta_t)\) and draw \(y_t \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p_t)\), where \(y_t=1\) might represent “recession this month.” Plot \(p_t\) together with the observed \(y_t\).
The observation equation is Bernoulli, not Gaussian, so the linear-Gaussian Kalman filter of the previous exercise no longer gives a closed-form posterior for \(\theta_t\). Implement a bootstrap particle filter: represent the filtering distribution of \(\theta_t\) with \(N\) weighted particles \(\theta_t^{(i)}\), propagate each particle through the random-walk transition, reweight it by the Bernoulli likelihood of \(y_t\), and resample. Report the filtered probability \(\hat p_t = \E{p_t \mid y_{1:t}} \approx \sum_i w_t^{(i)}\,\mathrm{logit}^{-1}(\theta_t^{(i)})\).
Compute the mean absolute tracking error \(\frac{1}{T}\sum_t |\hat p_t - p_t|\) and compare it to a naive baseline that always predicts the unconditional mean \(\bar y\). Report both numbers.
Refit the filter assuming a process noise \(\sigma_w = 0.05\), understating the true value. Does the filtered probability lag behind the true swings in \(p_t\)? Report the new tracking error and explain the result using the Kalman-gain intuition from the previous exercise.



Exercise 15.9 (Regime-Switching Volatility for S&P 500 Returns via Baum-Welch and Viterbi) The chapter’s HMM and regime-switching sections describe a hidden Markov chain \(x_t\) that switches the parameters of an observation process, \(y_t = \mu(x_t) + \sigma(x_t)\varepsilon_t\), and note that FFBS-type recursions can be adapted to estimate such models. Here you fit a two-regime Gaussian HMM to real financial data by implementing scaled Baum-Welch (EM) and Viterbi decoding from scratch (Baum et al. 1970; Viterbi 1967).

Load data/GSPC.csv (daily S&P 500 prices, already used in this chapter) and compute daily log returns \(r_t = 100(\log p_t - \log p_{t-1})\).
Implement Baum-Welch for a two-state Gaussian HMM, \(r_t \mid x_t = j \sim N(\mu_j, \sigma_j^2)\), with unknown transition matrix \(P\), unknown \((\mu_j, \sigma_j)\), and unknown initial distribution. Use scaled forward-backward recursions (dividing by \(c_t = p(y_t \mid y_{1:t-1})\) at each step, as in the chapter’s filtering recursions) to avoid underflow, iterating the E-step and M-step until the log-likelihood \(\sum_t \log c_t\) changes by less than \(10^{-6}\). Initialize by splitting returns into a near-median 70 percent group (low-volatility) and an extreme 30 percent group (high-volatility).
Label the state with the smaller \(\sigma_j\) as low-volatility and the other as high-volatility. Report the fitted transition matrix, the state-dependent mean and standard deviation of daily returns, and the expected regime duration \(1/(1 - P_{jj})\) in trading days for each regime.
Decode the Viterbi path and plot the filtered probability \(\prob{x_t = \text{high-vol} \mid y_{1:t}}\) over time. Report the mean filtered high-volatility probability during the COVID crash window (Feb 15 to Apr 15, 2020) versus calendar year 2017, and comment on whether the model isolates the crash as a distinct regime.



Exercise 15.10 (Quantile Regression Forests for Predictive Intervals) The chapter’s discussion of quantile regression forests shows how a random forest can estimate the full conditional distribution \(\hat p(y \mid x)\), not just the conditional mean \(\E{Y \mid X}\), by keeping track of which training values land in each leaf. Here you fit one on simulated heteroskedastic data and check whether its predictive intervals are actually calibrated.

Simulate \(n=800\) points with \(x \sim \text{Uniform}(0,10)\) and \(y = 3 + 2\sin(x) + \varepsilon\), where \(\varepsilon \sim N(0, \sigma(x)^2)\) and \(\sigma(x) = 0.4 + 0.35x\) grows with \(x\). Split into a training set (first 600 points) and a test set (last 200 points).
Check whether the ranger package is installed with requireNamespace(). If so, fit a quantile regression forest with quantreg = TRUE and predict the 10th, 50th, and 90th percentiles of \(y \mid x\) on the test set using predict(..., type = "quantiles"). If only quantregForest is available, use it instead. If neither package is installed, fall back to ordinary least squares plus the empirical quantiles of the training residuals, and note that this fallback only calibrates the interval on average, not conditionally on \(x\).
Using the 10th and 90th percentile predictions as an 80% interval, compute its empirical coverage: the fraction of test points whose \(y\) falls between the two predicted quantiles. How close is it to the nominal 0.80?
Now build a naive constant-width interval: add the 10th and 90th percentile of the training residuals to the median prediction, so every test point gets the same interval width. Compute the coverage of both intervals separately for \(x<3\) and for \(x>7\). Which method stays close to 80% coverage in both regions, and which one over-covers where the noise is small and under-covers where the noise is large?

title: 15  Forecasting
16  Model Selection
text:
16.1 Fundamental Considerations in Model Selection
Model selection is the art of choosing the model that best captures the true signal while avoiding the trap of fitting noise. Holmes’ words apply directly: when confronted with data, we must navigate countless possible models, each representing a different hypothesis, and systematically eliminate those that fail to generalize.
The next chapter (Chapter 17) covers regularization techniques (Ridge regression, LASSO, and their Bayesian interpretations), which can also be viewed as model selection mechanisms. Here we focus on the fundamental considerations: the bias-variance tradeoff, overfitting and underfitting, computational constraints, and whether our goal is prediction or interpretation. We draw on Breiman’s influential distinction between the “two cultures” of statistical modeling, then develop practical methodologies including cross-validation and information criteria.
In 2019, Obermeyer and colleagues examined a health risk score used to identify patients for extra care. Black patients were sicker than White patients assigned the same score. The algorithm predicted medical spending, and less was spent on Black patients at a given level of illness. The authors estimated that correcting the disparity would raise the Black share of patients automatically identified for extra care at the 97th percentile cutoff from 17.7% to 46.5% (Obermeyer et al. 2019).
The choice of outcome had made access to treatment part of a supposed measure of need. More records from the same billing system would preserve that mismatch. A smaller sample with reliable measures of illness and better coverage of underserved patients could be more useful. Even with a suitable target, a rigid model can underfit, missing interactions between illnesses, while a flexible model can overfit peculiarities of one clinic. The out-of-sample comparisons developed below assess whether the patterns a model learns carry over to new patients.
Choosing an outcome still leaves the decision about whom to enroll. With a fixed number of places, missing a patient who needs help and allocating a place to someone who needs it less have different consequences. Equal enrollment rates across groups and equal chances of enrollment among patients who need help can favor different rules. The health system must choose which disparities it aims to reduce and examine the resulting errors. Clinicians also need to explain why a particular patient was passed over, check for faulty records, and challenge inappropriate predictors. A small tree may make that review easier than a large network, even when their predictive performance is similar.
Any improvement from a larger network must also justify the cost of using it. Training cost is only part of the bill: serving predictions repeatedly consumes memory and computation. Quantization can replace 32-bit weights with 8-bit values, reducing their raw storage by a factor of four. Pruning removes selected weights or units; whether it speeds up prediction depends on the hardware and implementation. The compressed model needs fresh evaluation, including whether its errors have shifted disproportionately onto one patient group.
A compact model may also allow computation to stay within the health system, reducing transfers of confidential records. The fitted model itself can still disclose information about its training patients. Differential privacy bounds how much the distribution of released results can change when one person’s data are added or removed. Calibrated noise is one way to obtain that protection; stronger protection may reduce predictive accuracy (Dwork and Roth 2014). It must also decide how much privacy protection to require and who is responsible for the deployed model. That responsibility includes monitoring whom the model leaves out and giving patients a way to correct records and challenge decisions.

title: 16  Model Selection
text:
16.2 Prediction vs Interpretation
Predictive models can serve two distinct purposes: prediction and interpretation. These goals often conflict. Interpretation requires understanding the relationship between input and output variables, which typically demands simpler, more transparent models.
A model that excels at prediction might not be suitable for interpretation. For example, a complex deep neural network might achieve high predictive accuracy but provide little insight into how the input variables influence the output. Conversely, a simple linear model might be highly interpretable but lack the flexibility to capture complex relationships in the data. A key advantage of linear models is their ability to serve both purposes effectively, unlike more complex models with many parameters that can be difficult to interpret.
Interpretation problems typically require simpler models. We prioritize models that are easy to interpret and explain, even if they have slightly lower predictive accuracy. The evaluation metrics also differ: for interpretation, we typically use the coefficient of determination (R-squared) or \(p\)-values, which provide insights into the model’s fit and the statistical significance of the estimated relationships.
The choice between using a model for prediction or interpretation depends on the specific task and desired outcome. If the primary goal is accurate predictions, a complex model with high predictive accuracy might be preferred, even if it is less interpretable. However, if understanding the underlying relationships and causal mechanisms is crucial, a simpler and more interpretable model might be chosen, even if it has slightly lower predictive accuracy. Interpretive models are commonly used in scientific research, social sciences, and other fields where understanding the underlying causes and relationships is crucial.
In practice, it’s often beneficial to consider both prediction and interpretation when building and evaluating models. However, it is not unusual to build two different models, one for prediction and one for interpretation.

Breiman’s Two Cultures
Let \(x\) be a high-dimensional input containing a large set of potentially relevant data, and let \(y\) represent an output (or response) to a task that we aim to solve based on the information in \(x\). Breiman (2001b) summarizes the difference between statistical and machine learning philosophy as follows:

“There are two cultures in the use of statistical modeling to reach conclusions from data. One assumes that the data are generated by a given stochastic data model. The other uses algorithmic models and treats the data mechanism as unknown.”


“The statistical community has been committed to the almost exclusive use of data models. This commitment has led to irrelevant theory, questionable conclusions, and has kept statisticians from working on a large range of interesting current problems.”


“Algorithmic modeling, both in theory and practice, has developed rapidly in fields outside statistics. It can be used both on large complex data sets and as a more accurate and informative alternative to data modeling on smaller data sets. If our goal as a field is to use data to solve problems, then we need to move away from exclusive dependence on data models and adopt a more diverse set of tools.”

Deep learning predictors offer several advantages over traditional predictors:

Input data can include all data of possible relevance to the prediction problem at hand
Nonlinearities and complex interactions among input data are accounted for seamlessly
Fast, scalable computational frameworks (such as TensorFlow) are available

Tree-based models and deep learning models exemplify the “algorithmic culture” that Breiman describes. These models can capture complex, non-linear relationships in data without requiring explicit specification of the functional form. However, this flexibility comes at the cost of interpretability. While decision trees offer some interpretability through their hierarchical structure, deep neural networks are often considered “black boxes” due to their complex, multi-layered architecture.
The trade-off between interpretability and accuracy is a central theme in modern machine learning. Simple models like linear regression are highly interpretable but may lack the flexibility to capture complex patterns. Complex models like deep neural networks can achieve high accuracy but are difficult to interpret. This has led to the development of various techniques for making complex models more interpretable, including feature importance measures, attention mechanisms, and surrogate models that approximate the behavior of complex models with simpler, more interpretable ones.

title: 16  Model Selection
text:
16.3 Diagnostics for Model Assumptions
What makes a good model? If the goal is prediction, then the model is as good as its predictions. The easiest way to visualize the quality of predictions is to plot \(y\) versus \(\hat{y}\). Most of the time we use empirical assessment of model quality. However, sometimes theoretical bounds can be derived for a model that describe its accuracy. For example, in the case of the simple linear regression model, the prediction interval is defined by \[
\hat{y} \pm t_{n-2,\,1-\alpha/2}\, s\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{n}+\frac{(x-\bar{x})^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar{x})^2}}
\] where \(t_{n-2,\,1-\alpha/2}\) is the \(1-\alpha/2\) quantile of the t distribution with \(n-2\) degrees of freedom, which gives the interval coverage \(1-\alpha\), and \(s\) is the standard deviation of the residuals, \(s^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i-\hat{y}_i)^2/(n-2)\). The prediction interval covers a new observation \(y\) at \(x\). It is wider than the confidence interval for the mean response because it also includes the noise of the new observation, the \(1\) under the square root.
Assume we have a predictive model \[
y = f(x) + \epsilon
\] and we have some modeling assumption regarding the distribution of \(\epsilon\). For example, when we use linear regression or BART, we assume that \(\epsilon\) follows a normal distribution. One simple approach to check whether the residuals \(\hat\epsilon_1,\ldots,\hat\epsilon_n\) follow a specific distribution is Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA).
The most common tools for exploratory data analysis are Q-Q plots, scatter plots, and bar plots/histograms.
A Q-Q plot compares the quantiles of your data with the quantiles of a theoretical distribution (like normal, exponential, etc.). A quantile is the value below which a given fraction (or percent) of the points lie. That is, the \(i\)-th quantile is the point \(x\) for which \(i\)% of the data lie below \(x\). On a Q-Q plot, if the two datasets come from a population with the same distribution, we should see the points forming a line that’s roughly straight. More precisely, if the two datasets \(x\) and \(y\) come from the same distribution, then the points \((x_{(i)}, y_{(i)})\), where \(x_{(i)}\) is the \(i\)-th smallest value, should lie roughly on the line \(y = x\). If \(y\) has the distribution of a linear function of \(x\), then the points \((x_{(i)}, y_{(i)})\) should lie roughly on a line, but not necessarily on the line \(y = x\).

Example 16.1 (Normal Q-Q Plot) Figure 16.1 shows the normal Q-Q plot for the data on birth weights of babies born in a Brisbane hospital on December 18, 1997. The dataset contains 44 records. A more detailed description of the dataset can be found in UsingR manual.

babyboom <- read.csv("data/babyboom.csv")
qqnorm(babyboom$wt, bg = "lightblue", main = "", ylab = "Weight (g)")
qqline(babyboom$wt, col = "red", lwd = 3)







Figure 16.1: Normal Q-Q plot of baby weights.





Visual inspection of the Q-Q plot strongly suggests that birth weights are not normally distributed. We can see that on the left side of the plot the points are below the line. This indicates that the data are skewed to the left.
The Q-Q plots look different if we split the data based on gender.











(a) Girls











(b) Boys







Figure 16.2: Normal Q-Q plots of baby weights by gender.



How about the number of births per hour?

hr <- ceiling(babyboom$running.time / 60)
BirthsByHour <- tabulate(hr)
# Number of hours with 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 births
ObservedCounts <- table(BirthsByHour)
# Average number of births per hour
BirthRate <- sum(BirthsByHour) / 24
# Expected counts for Poisson distribution, the last bin holds 4 or more births
ExpectedCounts <- c(dpois(0:3, BirthRate), ppois(3, BirthRate, lower.tail = FALSE)) * 24
# bind into matrix for plotting
ObsExp <- rbind(ObservedCounts, ExpectedCounts)
barplot(ObsExp, names = c(0:3, "4+"), beside = TRUE, legend = c("Observed", "Expected"),
        xlab = "Births per hour", ylab = "Number of hours")




Number of hours with a given number of births: observed and expected under a Poisson distribution.




What about the Q-Q plot?

# birth intervals
birthinterval <- diff(babyboom$running.time)
# quantiles of standard exponential distribution (rate=1)
exponential.quantiles <- qexp(ppoints(43))
qqplot(exponential.quantiles, birthinterval, bg = "lightblue",
       xlab = "Exponential quantiles", ylab = "Time between births (minutes)")
lmb <- mean(birthinterval)
lines(exponential.quantiles, exponential.quantiles * lmb, col = 2) # Overlay a line




Exponential Q-Q plot of the times between births.




Here

ppoints function computes the sequence of probability points
qexp function computes the quantiles of the exponential distribution
diff function computes the difference between consecutive elements of a vector

title: 16  Model Selection
text:
16.4 Out-of-Sample Performance
A parametric model is selected from a family of functions, with optimization finding the best member by minimizing empirical loss or maximizing likelihood. Finding the right family is the model selection problem: which predictors, interactions, or transformations achieve the best balance between complexity and accuracy? In practice, several models often perform nearly identically.
The optimal model is rarely the one that fits training data perfectly, which typically indicates overfitting, where the model captures noise rather than signal. A good model balances fit against simplicity to ensure generalization.
The goal of model selection is not only to achieve a good fit but also to reduce complexity by excluding unnecessary parameters. This process typically involves selecting a model from a relevant class of functions while keeping in mind the trade-offs between bias, variance, and model complexity. Techniques such as cross-validation, information criteria (e.g., AIC (Akaike 1974), BIC), and regularization methods are commonly used to guide the model selection process.
The model selection task is sometimes one of the most time-consuming parts of data analysis. Unfortunately, there is no single rule to find the best model. One way to think about the model choice problem is as yet another optimization problem, with the goal of finding the best family of functions that describe the data. With a small number of predictors, we can use brute force (check all possible models). For example, with \(p\) predictors there are \(2^p\) possible models with no interactions. Thus, the number of potential function families is huge even for modest values of \(p\). One cannot consider all transformations and interactions.
Our goal is to build a model that predicts well for out-of-sample data, i.e., data that was not used for training. Ultimately, we are interested in using our models for prediction, and thus out-of-sample performance is the most important metric and should be used to choose the final model. In-sample performance is of little interest when choosing a predictive model: it is like predicting how much someone will like a movie after having them watch it and tell you how much they really liked it. The goal is to use data to find a pattern that we can exploit. The pattern will be “statistical” in nature. To uncover the pattern, we start with a training dataset, denoted by \[
D = (y_i,x_i)_{i=1}^n
\] and to test the validity of our model, we use an out-of-sample testing dataset \[
D^* = (y_j^*, x_j^*)_{j=1}^m,
\] where \(x_i\) is a set of \(p\) predictors and \(y_i\) is the response variable.
A good predictor will “generalize” well and provide low MSE out-of-sample. There are a number of methods and objective functions that we will use to find \(\hat{f}\). Our goal is to find the map \(f\) that approximates the process that generated the data. For example, data could represent some physical observations, and our goal is to recover the “laws of nature” that led to those observations. One of the pitfalls is to find a map \(f\) that does not generalize. Generalization means that our model actually learned the “laws of nature” and not just identified patterns present in training. The lack of generalization of the model is called overfitting. It can be demonstrated in one dimension by remembering the fact from calculus that any set of \(n\) points with distinct \(x\) values can be interpolated by a polynomial of degree \(n-1\), e.g., we can always draw a line that connects two points. Thus, in one dimension we can always find a function with zero empirical risk. However, such a function is unlikely to generalize to observations that were not in our training data. The empirical risk measure for \(D^*\) is likely to be very high.

Example 16.2 (Hard Function) Say we want to approximate the following function \[
f(x) = \dfrac{1}{1+25x^2}.
\] This function is simply a ratio of two polynomial functions, and we will try to build a linear model to reconstruct this function:

x <- seq(-2, 2, by = 0.01)
y <- 1 / (1 + 25 * x^2)
# Approximate with polynomial of degree 1 and 2
m1 <- lm(y ~ x)
m2 <- lm(y ~ poly(x, 2))
# Approximate with polynomial of degree 20 and 5
m20 <- lm(y ~ poly(x, 20))
m5 <- lm(y ~ poly(x, 5))









Figure 16.3: Runge function (solid) and polynomial fits of degree 1, 2, 5 and 20. The vertical lines mark the training interval.





Figure 16.3 shows the function itself (solid black line) on the interval \([-3,3]\). We used observations of \(x\) from the interval \([-2,2]\) to train the data (between the vertical lines) and from \([-3,-2) \cup (2,3]\) (outside them) to test the model and measure the out-of-sample performance. We tried four different linear functions to capture the relations. We see that the linear model \(\hat{y} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x\) is not a good model. However, as we increase the degree of the polynomial to 20, the resulting model \(\hat{y} = \beta_0 + \beta_1x + \beta_2 x^2 +\ldots+\beta_{20}x^{20}\) does fit the training dataset quite well, but does a very poor job on the test dataset. Thus, while in-sample performance is good, the out-of-sample performance is unsatisfactory. We should not use the degree 20 polynomial function as a predictive model. In practice, in-sample loss or classification rates provide us with a metric for comparing different predictors. There should be a penalty for overly complex rules that fit extremely well in-sample but perform poorly on out-of-sample data. As a dictum often attributed to Einstein puts it, “A model should be simple, but not simpler.”

To a Bayesian, the solutions to statistical decision problems (estimation, prediction and model choice) are rather obvious: compute posterior distributions, and then make decisions by maximizing expected utility, where the posterior distribution is used to calculate the expectations. Classical solutions to these problems are different, and use repeated sampling ideas, whereby the performance of a decision rule is judged on its performance if the same decision problem were repeated infinitely. Thus, the decisions are made based on their population properties. One of the main uses of statistical decision theory is to compare different estimators or hypothesis testing procedures. This theory generates many important findings, most notably that many of the common classical estimators are “bad”, in some sense, and that Bayesian estimators under a proper prior are “good”, namely admissible (under mild conditions; Bayes rules from improper priors carry no such guarantee).

title: 16  Model Selection
text:
16.5 Bias-Variance Trade-off
For any predictive model, we seek to achieve the best possible results, i.e., the smallest MSE or misclassification rate. For a historical perspective on how aggregating independent estimates reduces variance while preserving low bias, see the discussion of Galton’s ox-weighing experiment in Section 10.1.5. However, model performance can vary depending on the specific training/validation split used. A model that performed well on one test set may not produce good results given additional data. Sometimes we observe situations where a small change in the data leads to a large change in the final estimated model, e.g., the parameters of the model. These results exemplify the bias/variance tradeoff, where increasing model bias can reduce variance in the final results. Similarly, low bias can result in high variance. Figure 16.4 illustrates the trade-off.






Figure 16.4: Bias-variance trade-off




Example 16.3 (Bias-variance) We demonstrate bias-variance concept using Boston housing example. We fit a model \(\mathrm{medv} = f(\mathrm{lstat})\). We use polynomial functions to approximate this relation. We fitted twelve polynomial functions with degree \(1,\ldots,12\) one hundred times. Each time we randomly selected 20% of the sample for testing and the rest for training. We estimated in-sample and out-of-sample performance by calculating MSE on training and testing sets correspondingly. For each polynomial \(f\) we took the mean of the in-sample MSE and the median of the out-of-sample MSE, because a few extreme values of lstat in a test set make the mean of a high degree polynomial explode.
Figure 16.5 (a) shows in-sample MSE and model variance, the variance of the predictions across fits, for our twelve different models. As expected, in-sample MSE, which reflects the falling bias, decreases while variance increases as model complexity grows. On the other hand out-of-sample MSE is a U-shaped curve. The optimal model is the one that has smallest out-of-sample MSE. In our case, it is a polynomial of degree 5.











(a) Bias-Variance











(b) Optimal complexity model.







Figure 16.5: Metrics for twelve polynomial functions fitted into Boston housing dataset. Left panel: As model complexity (degree of the polynomial function) increases, model variance increases and in-sample MSE decreases. Out-of-sample MSE is smallest for 5th degree polynomial function, which is the optimal model in terms of bias-variance trade-off. Right panel: Optimal model, which is 5th degree polynomial used to predict observations from testing dataset. Model predictions (solid line) are compared to actual observed values of medv variable (dots).



Let’s take another, more formal look at the bias-variance trade-off for a linear regression problem. We are interested in the decomposition of the error \(\E{(y-\hat{y})^2}\) as a function of bias \(\E{y-\hat{y}}\) and variance \(\Var{\hat{y}}\).
Here \(\hat{y} = \hat{f}_{\beta}(x)\) is the prediction from the model, and \(y = f(x) + \epsilon\) is the true value, which is measured with noise \(\Var{\epsilon} = \sigma^2\), where \(f(x)\) is the true unknown function. The expectation above is at a fixed input \(x\), over the noise of a new observation \(y\) and over the training sets that produce \(\hat{y}\). The new noise \(\epsilon\) is independent of the training data, so \(y\) and \(\hat{y}\) are independent. \[
\begin{aligned}
\E{(y - \hat{y})^2}
& = \E{y^2 + \hat{y}^2 - 2 y\hat{y}} \\
& = \E{y^2} + \E{\hat{y}^2} - \E{2y\hat{y}} \\
& = \Var{y} + \E{y}^2 + \Var{\hat{y}} + \E{\hat{y}}^2 - 2f\E{\hat{y}} \\
& = \Var{y} + \Var{\hat{y}} + (f^2 - 2f\E{\hat{y}} + \E{\hat{y}}^2) \\
& = \Var{y} + \Var{\hat{y}} + (f - \E{\hat{y}})^2 \\
& = \sigma^2 + \Var{\hat{y}} + \mathrm{Bias}(\hat{y})^2\end{aligned}
\] Here we used the following identity: \(\Var{X} = \E{X^2} - \E{X}^2\) and the fact that \(f\) is deterministic and \(\E{\epsilon} = 0\), thus \(\E{y} = \E{f(x)+\epsilon} = f + \E{\epsilon} = f\).

title: 16  Model Selection
text:
16.6 Cross-Validation
If the dataset at hand is small and we cannot dedicate a large enough sample size for testing, simply measuring error on a test dataset can lead to wrong conclusions. When the size of the testing set \(D^*\) is small, the estimated out-of-sample performance has high variance, depending on precisely which observations are included in the test set. On the other hand, when the training set \(D\) is a small fraction of the entire sample available, the out-of-sample error is overestimated, because the model is fitted on fewer observations than the final model will use.
A simple solution is to perform the training/testing split randomly several times and then use the average out-of-sample errors. This procedure has two parameters: the fraction of samples to be selected for testing \(q\) and the number of estimates to be performed \(K\). The resulting algorithm is as follows:
set.seed(1)
fsz = as.integer(q*n)
error = rep(0,K)
for (k in 1:K)
{
    test_ind = sample(1:n,size = fsz)
    training = d[-test_ind,]
    testing = d[test_ind,]
    m = lm(y~x, data=training)
    yhat = predict(m,newdata = testing)
    error[k] = mean((yhat-testing$y)^2)
}
res = mean(error)
Figure 16.6 shows the process of splitting the dataset randomly five times.
Cross-validation (Stone 1974) modifies the random splitting approach to use a more “disciplined” way to split the dataset for training and testing. Instead of randomly selecting training data points, CV shuffles the observations once and splits them into \(K\) consecutive blocks (folds), and thus each data point is used once for testing. Like the random approach, CV helps address the high variance issue of out-of-sample performance estimation when the available dataset is small. Figure 16.7 shows the process of splitting the dataset five times using the cross-validation approach.









Figure 16.6: Bootstrap











Figure 16.7: Cross-validation







Training set (dark squares) and testing set (light squares)




Example 16.4 (Simulated) We use a simulated dataset to demonstrate the difference between estimated out-of-sample performance using random 20/80 split, 5-fold cross-validation and bootstrap. We used \(x=-2,-1.99,-1.98,\ldots,2\) and \(y = 2+3x + \epsilon, ~ \epsilon \sim N(0,\sqrt{3})\). We simulated 35 datasets of size 100. For each of the simulated datasets, we fitted a linear model and estimated out-of-sample performance using three different approaches. Figure 16.8 compares empirical distribution of errors estimated from 35 samples.






Figure 16.8: Empirical comparison of simple split, cross-validation, and bootstrap approaches to estimate out-of-sample performance.



As we can see the estimated out-of-sample performance by a training set approach is of high variance. While both cross-validation and bootstrap approaches lead to better estimates, they require the model to be fitted 5 times, which can be computationally costly for a complex model. On the other hand, estimate from cross-validation is of lower variance and less bias compared to the bootstrap estimate. Thus, we should prefer cross-validation.

title: 16  Model Selection
section: 16.7 Model Evaluation: Calibration, Discrimination, and Scoring
text:
16.7 Model Evaluation: Calibration, Discrimination, and Scoring
Variable selection is often presented as choosing a subset of predictors. A complementary view is that we are searching for a low-dimensional summary of the inputs that retains predictive information: an informal analogue of the idea of a minimal sufficient statistic from classical inference (Chapter 3).
When we evaluate models, it is useful to separate three questions. First, does the model rank or separate cases well (discrimination)? Second, do the model’s predicted probabilities match observed frequencies (calibration)? Third, when we must make decisions, how should we score probabilistic forecasts so that “better” means “closer to the truth” in a principled way?
For binary outcomes, discrimination is often summarized by the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve. For a thresholded score, define the true positive rate (TPR, the share of actual positives classified as positive) and false positive rate (FPR, the share of actual negatives classified as positive) as the threshold varies. The ROC curve plots TPR against FPR across all thresholds, and the area under the curve (AUC) summarizes performance as a single number between 0 and 1, with 0.5 corresponding to random ranking; see Fawcett (2006).

Calibration and Calibration Plots
Calibration concerns the probabilistic interpretation of predicted probabilities. A well-calibrated model that outputs \(\hat p=0.8\) in many cases should be correct about 80% of the time in those cases. A common diagnostic is a calibration plot (reliability diagram), which bins predictions and compares average predicted probability to the empirical frequency in each bin.


Proper Scoring Rules (and the Decision-Theory Link)
A proper scoring rule assigns a numerical score to a probabilistic forecast and is designed so that, in expectation, the best strategy is to report the true predictive distribution; see Gneiting and Raftery (2007). Two widely used examples are the log score (negative log predictive density) and the Brier score for binary outcomes Brier (1950). These connect directly to Chapter 4: choosing a scoring rule is equivalent to choosing a loss for probabilistic prediction, and the expected score becomes a decision-theoretic risk.


Posterior Predictive Checks
For Bayesian models, posterior predictive checks compare observed data to replicated data drawn from the posterior predictive distribution. The workflow is: sample parameters from the posterior, simulate replicated datasets, and compare summary statistics or discrepancies between observed and replicated data; see Rubin (1984).

title: 16  Model Selection
text:
16.8 Bayesian Model Selection
The probabilistic models of interest are the joint probability distribution \(p(D,\theta)\) (called a generative model) and \(P(Y,\theta \mid X)\) (discriminative model). Discriminative models are easier to build and are more frequently used in practice. Generative models require modeling a distribution over the set of observed variables, which makes our model more complicated. Text analysis provides an illustrative example. The task of identifying the topic of an article can be solved using a discriminative distribution. The problem of generating a new article requires a generative model.
Let \(D\) denote data. Let \(\theta_M \in \Theta_M\) denote a set of parameters under model \(M \in \mathcal{M}\). Let \(\theta_M = (\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_p)\) be the \(p\)-vector of parameters. The Bayesian approach is straightforward: implement the Bayesian paradigm by executing Bayes’ rule. This requires the laws of probability and not optimization techniques. The notion of model complexity is no different. Let \(\mathcal{M}\) denote the space of models and \(\theta\) be the parameter vector. The Bayesian paradigm simply places probabilities over parameters and models given the data, namely \(p(\theta_M, M \mid y)\), where \(y = (y_1, \ldots, y_n)\).
This has a number of decompositions. Bayes’ theorem calculates the joint posterior over parameters and models given data \(D\), namely \[
    p(\theta_M,M\mid D) = p(\theta_M \mid M,D)P(M\mid D).
\] Notice how this factors the posterior into two terms: the conditional posterior over parameters given the model and the posterior over models given data.
The key quantity is the evidence (a.k.a. the marginal likelihood, the marginal distribution of the data \(D\) given the model \(M\)), defined by \[
p(D \mid M) = \int_{\Theta_M} p(D \mid \theta_M, M) p(\theta_M \mid M) d\theta_M.
\] Here \(p(D \mid \theta_M, M)\) is the traditional likelihood function. The key conditional distribution, however, is the specification of the prior over parameters \(p(\theta_M \mid M)\). As this is used in the marginalization, it can affect the Bayes risk dramatically. Occam’s razor comes from the fact that this marginalization gives an evidence that favors simpler models over more complex ones.
This leads to a posterior over models, which is calculated as: \[\begin{align*}
    P(M\mid D)  & = \dfrac{p(D\mid M)P(M)}{p(D)}, \\
    p(D\mid M ) & = \int_{ \Theta_M} p(D\mid \theta_M , M ) p( \theta_M \mid M ) d \theta_M.
\end{align*}\] Notice that this requires a joint prior specification \(p(\theta_M, M) = p(\theta_M \mid M)p(M)\) over parameters and models. The quantity \(p(M \mid D)\) is the marginal posterior for model complexity given the data. There is an equivalent posterior \(p(\theta_M \mid D)\) for the parameters. \(p(D \mid M)\) is the evidence of the data \(D\) given the model. The full evidence is \[
p( D ) = \int p( D \mid M ) p(M) d M.
\] This has been used to select the amount of hyperparameter regularization; see, for example, D. J. MacKay (1992).
We will see that the prior \(p(\theta_M \mid M)\) will lead to an Occam’s razor effect, namely that the marginal distribution will favor simpler models. Importantly, this Occam’s razor effect is not in conflict with the Bayesian double descent phenomenon (Section 19.8), which emerges from the marginal posterior of models given data and the conditional prior specification \(p(\theta_M \mid M)\).

This example shows how Bayes’ rule weighs competing models by the probability each assigns to the observed data. A flexible model spreads its probability over more possible data sets, so for a given data set it receives lower evidence than a simpler model that explains the data equally well. This penalty is called the automatic Occam’s razor. Occam’s razor is a principle that states that the simplest explanation is the best explanation.
