title: 20  Gradient Descent
text:
20.2 Stochastic Gradient Descent
Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is a variant of the gradient descent algorithm. The main difference is that instead of computing the gradient over the entire dataset, SGD computes the gradient over a randomly selected subset of the data. This allows SGD to be applied to estimate models when the dataset is too large to fit into memory, which is often the case with deep learning models. The SGD algorithm replaces the gradient of the negative log-likelihood function with the gradient computed over a randomly selected subset of the data: \[
    \nabla l(\theta) \approx \dfrac{1}{|B|} \sum_{i \in B} \nabla l(y_i, f(x_i, \theta)),
\] where \(B \subseteq \{1,2,\ldots,n\}\) is a batch (random subset) sampled from the dataset, and \(|B|\) denotes the batch size (number of samples in the batch). This method can be interpreted as gradient descent using noisy gradients, which are typically called mini-batch gradients.
SGD is based on the idea of stochastic approximation introduced by Robbins and Monro (1951). Stochastic approximation simply replaces the expected gradient with its Monte Carlo approximation.
In a small mini-batch regime, when \(|B| \ll n\) and typically \(|B| \in \{32,64,\ldots,1024\}\), it was shown that SGD needs less computation than standard gradient descent on large datasets and, with decreasing step sizes, converges to minimizers of strongly convex functions (the negative log-likelihood of an exponential-family model is convex in its natural parameter, and strongly convex under \(L_2\) regularization) (Bottou, Curtis, and Nocedal 2018), and that it generalizes stably when trained for few epochs (Hardt, Recht, and Singer 2016). Further, gradient methods with added noise can escape saddle points (Ge et al. 2015; Jin et al. 2017), which are often an issue with deep learning loss functions. In the case of multiple minima, SGD can find a good solution (LeCun et al. 1998), and out-of-sample performance is often worse when trained with large-batch methods compared to small-batch methods (Keskar et al. 2016).
Now, we implement SGD for logistic regression and compare performance for different batch sizes

lrgd_minibatch  = function(x,y, alpha, n_iter, bs) {
  theta <- matrix(c(0, 0), nrow = 2, ncol = n_iter+1)
  n = length(y)
  for (i in 1:n_iter) {
    s = ((i-1)*bs+1)%%n
    e = min(s+bs-1,n)
    xl = x[s:e,]; yl = y[s:e]
    p = 1/(1+exp(-xl %*% theta[,i]))
    grad <- -t(xl) %*% (yl - p)
    # update theta
    theta[,i+1] <- theta[,i] - alpha * grad
  }
  return(theta)
}

Now run our SGD algorithm with different batch sizes.

set.seed(92)
ind = sample(150)
y = ifelse(iris$Species=="setosa",1,0)[ind] # shuffle data
x = cbind(rep(1,150),iris$Sepal.Length)[ind,] # shuffle data
nit=200000
lr = 0.01
th1 = lrgd_minibatch(x,y,lr,nit,5)
th2 = lrgd_minibatch(x,y,lr,nit,15)
th3 = lrgd_minibatch(x,y,lr,nit,30)








We run it with 200000 iterations and the learning rate of 0.01 and plot the intercept \(\theta_0\) every 100 iterations. First, we shuffle the data before using it. The reason is that if the data are sorted in any way (e.g., by date or by value of one of the inputs), then data within batches can be highly correlated, which reduces the convergence speed. Shuffling helps avoid this issue, but it also implicitly treats the dataset as exchangeable; for time series and streaming data, shuffling is typically inappropriate (see Chapter 15). Second, the larger the batch size, the smaller the number of iterations required for convergence. This is an artifact of the code, which sums the gradient over the batch instead of averaging it as in the formula above, so the effective step is the learning rate times the batch size. With the average, the curves for different batch sizes nearly coincide at the same number of iterations. The code shuffles once and then cycles through fixed batches, and the dashed line is the glm estimate. Let’s look at the same plot, but scale the x-axis according to the amount of computations, which makes the curves nearly coincide










The larger the batch size, the more memory is required to store the data.
Parallelization is more efficient with larger batch sizes. Modern hardware supports parallelization of matrix operations, which is the main operation in SGD. Usually there is a sweet spot \(|B|\) for the batch size, which is the largest batch size that can fit into memory or be parallelized. This means it takes the same amount of time to compute an SGD step for batch size \(1\) and \(|B|\).
The larger the batch size, the less noise in the gradient. However, it was empirically shown that in many applications we should prefer noisier gradients (small batches) to obtain high-quality solutions when the objective function (negative log-likelihood) is non-convex (Keskar et al. 2016).

title: 20  Gradient Descent
text:
20.3 Automatic Differentiation (Backpropagation)
Gradient descent requires computing gradients at each iteration. But how do we efficiently compute gradients for complex compositional functions like deep neural networks? The answer lies in automatic differentiation, a technique whose development is intertwined with the history of neural networks themselves.
Original neural networks (Perceptrons) proposed by Rosenblatt (1958) were single-layer feedforward networks with a threshold activation function in the output layer. They were trained using an error-correction (perceptron) learning rule.
The delta rule goes back to the least mean squares rule of Widrow and Hoff (1960) for a linear unit and gives a simple gradient-based learning algorithm for single-layer networks with a differentiable activation. For a single-layer perceptron with output \(\hat{y} = \sigma(w^\top x + b)\) and squared-error loss \((\hat{y}-y)^2/2\), where \(\sigma\) is an activation function, the delta rule updates weights as: \[
w^{t+1} = w^t - \alpha (\hat{y} - y) \sigma'(w^\top x + b) x
\] where \(\alpha\) is the learning rate, and \(y\) is the target output. This rule is intuitive: when the prediction \(\hat{y}\) differs from the target \(y\), we adjust the weights proportionally to the input \(x\) and the derivative of the activation function.
However, the delta rule encounters a fundamental limitation with multi-layer networks. Consider a network with hidden layers: \(h = \sigma_1(W_1 x + b_1)\) and \(\hat{y} = \sigma_2(W_2 h + b_2)\). To update weight \(W_1\) in the first layer, we need to compute \(\frac{\partial L}{\partial W_1}\), where \(L\) is the loss function. By the chain rule: \[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial W_1} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \hat{y}} \cdot \frac{\partial \hat{y}}{\partial h} \cdot \frac{\partial h}{\partial W_1}
\]
The delta rule could not efficiently compute this gradient through multiple layers, as it lacked a systematic method for propagating error signals backward through the network. This meant that while single-layer networks could be trained effectively, there was no practical way to train deeper architectures that could learn more complex representations.
The inability to train multi-layer networks contributed to a decline of neural network research in the 1970s, part of what is called the first AI winter. Minsky and Papert (1969) demonstrated that single-layer perceptrons could not solve non-linearly separable problems like XOR, and without a method to train deeper architectures, neural network research largely stagnated.
Unknown to most of the neural network community at the time, the solution to training multi-layer networks through systematic application of the chain rule was being developed independently by several researchers. In the Soviet Union, Galushkin (1974) developed methods for training multi-layer networks using gradient-based approaches, though this work remained largely unknown in the West due to the Cold War.
In the neural network literature, the idea of using the chain rule to efficiently compute gradients in multi-layer networks goes back to the 1974 PhD thesis of Paul J. Werbos (1974) at Harvard University. Werbos explicitly showed how to propagate derivatives backward through a network by decomposing complex functions into simpler components. He refined these ideas further in Paul J. Werbos (1982), demonstrating how reverse-mode automatic differentiation could be applied to train neural networks efficiently.
The same mathematical principle, systematic application of the chain rule for computing derivatives, was being applied in a different context around the same time. Nelder and Wedderburn (1972) introduced Generalized Linear Models (GLMs) and developed an iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS) algorithm that explicitly used the chain rule to compute gradients for maximum likelihood estimation.
To understand their contribution, consider a GLM where the response variable \(y_i\) follows a distribution from the exponential family with mean \(\mu_i\). The model relates the mean to the predictors through a link function \(g(\cdot)\): \[
g(\mu_i) = \eta_i = x_i^\top \theta
\] where \(x_i\) is the vector of predictors for observation \(i\), \(\theta\) is the parameter vector, and \(\eta_i\) is the linear predictor. For example, in logistic regression (which we saw in Example 20.2), we have \(g(\mu) = \log(\mu/(1-\mu))\) (the logit link).
Computing the gradient of the log-likelihood with respect to \(\theta\) requires an application of the chain rule. Specifically, for observation \(i\), the gradient decomposes as: \[
\frac{\partial \log L_i}{\partial \theta_j} = \frac{\partial \log L_i}{\partial \mu_i} \cdot \frac{\partial \mu_i}{\partial \eta_i} \cdot \frac{\partial \eta_i}{\partial \theta_j}
\]
The first term, \(\partial \log L_i/\partial \mu_i\), depends on the specific distribution (e.g., Gaussian, Bernoulli, Poisson). For exponential family distributions, this takes the form \((y_i - \mu_i)/(\phi V(\mu_i))\) with dispersion \(\phi\), where \(V(\mu_i)\) is the variance function; we take \(\phi = 1\) below, since it cancels in the update. The second term, \(\partial \mu_i/\partial \eta_i\), is the derivative of the inverse link function. The third term is simply \(x_{ij}\), the \(j\)-th predictor value.
Combining these using the chain rule, they derived the gradient: \[
\frac{\partial \log L}{\partial \theta_j} = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{(y_i - \mu_i)}{V(\mu_i)} \cdot \frac{\partial \mu_i}{\partial \eta_i} \cdot x_{ij}
\]
For the Newton-Raphson optimization method (also known as Fisher scoring when using expected second derivatives), they needed to compute the Hessian matrix. Applying the chain rule again to the gradient yields the Fisher information matrix with elements: \[
\mathcal{I}_{jk} = \sum_{i=1}^n w_i x_{ij} x_{ik}
\] where the weight \(w_i = \left(\frac{\partial \mu_i}{\partial \eta_i}\right)^2 / V(\mu_i)\) is itself computed by the chain rule. This leads to the iteratively reweighted least squares algorithm, where at each iteration \(t\) we update: \[
\theta^{t+1} = \theta^t + \mathcal{I}(\theta^t)^{-1} \nabla \log L(\theta^t)
\]
The success of GLMs demonstrated that chain rule-based gradient computation was practically valuable for fitting sophisticated models. Nelder and Wedderburn published their GLM framework in 1972, just two years before Werbos’s PhD thesis on backpropagation. Backpropagation did not enter mainstream neural network research until Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams (1986) popularized it under the name backpropagation.
To calculate the value of the gradient vector at each step of the optimization process, gradient descent algorithms require calculations of derivatives. In general, there are four different ways to calculate those derivatives. First, we can do it by hand. This is slow and error-prone. Second is numerical differentiation, when a gradient is approximated by a finite difference; for some small \(h\), calculate \(f'(x) \approx (f(x+h)-f(x))/h\), which requires two function evaluations. This approach is numerically delicate (Griewank, Kulshreshtha, and Walther 2012): a large \(h\) gives truncation error and a small \(h\) gives rounding error from subtracting nearly equal numbers. Third, we can use symbolic differentiation, which has been used for decades in computer algebra systems such as Mathematica or Maple. Symbolic differentiation uses a tree form representation of a function and applies the chain rule to the tree to calculate the symbolic derivative of a given function.
The advantage of symbolic calculations is that the analytical representation of the derivative is available for further analysis, for example, when derivative calculation is an intermediate step of the analysis. A fourth way to calculate a derivative is to use automatic differentiation (AD). Similar to symbolic differentiation, AD recursively applies the chain rule and calculates the exact value of the derivative, thus avoiding the problem of numerical instability. The difference between AD and symbolic differentiation is that AD provides the value of the derivative evaluated at a specific point, rather than an analytical representation of the derivative.
AD does not require analytical specification and can be applied to a function defined by a sequence of algebraic manipulations, logical and transcendental functions applied to input variables and specified in computer code. AD can differentiate complex functions which involve if statements and loops, and AD can be implemented using either forward or backward mode. Consider an example of calculating a derivative of the logistic function \[
f(x) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-(Wx+b)}}.
\]
Which is implemented as follows:

sigmoid = function(x,b,w){
  v1 = w*x
  v2 = v1 + b
  v3 = 1/(1+exp(-v2))
}



Given the function \(f(x) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-(Wx+b)}} = v_3\), the derivative with respect to \(w\) is given by the chain rule. Recall that for the sigmoid function \(\sigma(z) = 1/(1+e^{-z})\), we have \(\sigma'(z) = \sigma(z)(1-\sigma(z))\). Therefore: \[
\frac{\partial f}{\partial w} = \frac{\partial v_3}{\partial v_2} \cdot \frac{\partial v_2}{\partial v_1} \cdot \frac{\partial v_1}{\partial w} = v_3(1-v_3) \cdot 1 \cdot x
\]
\[
\frac{\partial f}{\partial b} = \frac{\partial v_3}{\partial v_2} \cdot \frac{\partial v_2}{\partial b} = v_3(1-v_3) \cdot 1
\]
In the forward mode, an auxiliary variable, called a dual number, will be added to each line of the code to track the value of the derivative associated with this line. In our example, if we set x=2, w=3, b=-5, we get the calculations given in the table below.







Function calculations
Derivative calculations




1. v1 = w*x = 6
1. dv1 = w = 3 (derivative of v1 with respect to x)


2. v2 = v1 + b = 1
2. dv2 = dv1 = 3 (derivative of v2 with respect to x)


3. v3 = 1/(1+exp(-v2)) = 0.731
3. dv3 = dv2*v3*(1-v3) = 0.590



Variables dv1,dv2,dv3 correspond to partial (local) derivatives of each intermediate variable v1,v2,v3 with respect to \(x\), and are called dual variables. Tracking for dual variables can either be implemented using source code modification tools that add new code for calculating the dual numbers or via operator overloading.
The reverse AD also applies the chain rule recursively but starts from the outer function, as shown in the table below.







Function calculations
Derivative calculations




1. v1 = w*x = 6
4. dv1 = dv2*dv2dv1 = 0.197; df/dx = dv1*w = 0.590


2. v2 = v1 + b = 1
3. dv2dv1 = 1; dv2 = dv3*dv3dv2 = 0.197


3. v3 = 1/(1+exp(-v2)) = 0.731
2. dv3 = dv4 = 1; dv3dv2 = v3*(1-v3) = 0.197


4. v4 = v3
1. dv4 = 1



The key difference between forward and reverse mode is the direction of computation:






Figure 20.2: Comparison of forward and reverse mode automatic differentiation for \(f = \sigma(wx + b)\).




Forward mode: Propagates derivatives with the computation, from inputs to outputs. Efficient when number of inputs < number of outputs.
Reverse mode: Propagates derivatives against the computation, from outputs to inputs. Efficient when number of outputs < number of inputs.

For neural networks with millions of parameters (inputs to the loss function) but a single scalar loss (one output), reverse mode is dramatically more efficient, which is why backpropagation uses reverse mode AD.
Figure 20.3 shows a graph representation of the composition of affine and sigmoid functions (a single sigmoid unit). The numbers in the nodes are the values of the variables at a specific point, and the arrows show the flow of data. During the forward pass (solid arrows), the data flow from inputs (x, w, b) to the final output v3, and all intermediate variables are computed. During the backward pass (dashed arrows), the gradient values flow from the output back to the inputs by applying the chain rule to each variable.






Figure 20.3: Computational Graph for Sigmoid Function



For DL, derivatives are calculated by applying the reverse AD algorithm to a model which is defined as a composition of functions. A model is defined either using a general-purpose language as it is done in PyTorch or through a sequence of function calls defined by framework libraries (e.g., in TensorFlow). Forward AD algorithms calculate the derivative with respect to a single input variable, but reverse AD produces derivatives with respect to all intermediate variables. For models with many parameters, it is much more computationally feasible to perform the reverse AD.
In the context of neural networks, the reverse AD algorithm is called backpropagation and was popularized in AI by Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams (1986). According to Schmidhuber (2015), the first version of what we call today backpropagation was published in 1970 in a master’s thesis Linnainmaa (1970) and was closely related to the work of Ostrovskii, Volin, and Borisov (1971). However, similar techniques rooted in Pontryagin’s maximum principle were discussed in the context of multi-stage control problems (Arthur E. Bryson 1961; Arthur E. Bryson and Ho 1969). Dreyfus (1962) applies backpropagation to calculate the first-order derivative of a return function to numerically solve a variational problem. Later Dreyfus (1973) used backpropagation to derive an efficient algorithm to solve a minimization problem. According to the same survey, the idea appeared in Paul J. Werbos (1974) and the first neural network-specific application of efficient backpropagation in Paul J. Werbos (1982).
Modern deep learning frameworks fully automate the process of finding derivatives using AD algorithms. For example, PyTorch relies on the autograd library which automatically finds gradients using the backpropagation algorithm. Here is a small code example using the grad function of jax.
The code below implements a simple neural network with one hidden layer and uses backpropagation to find the gradient of the negative log-likelihood function. The model is trained on a synthetic dataset generated from a circle. The code uses the jax library, which is a high-performance numerical computing library that supports automatic differentiation. The 200 points x (two coordinates each) and their 0/1 labels y are read from data/circle.csv, and the weights and biases w1, b1 of the four hidden units and w2, b2 of the output unit start as small random normal numbers. A JAX random key gives the same numbers every time it is used, so the code splits one key into four, one per array; reusing a single key would make b1 a scaled copy of the first entries of w1. In the code, jnp stands for jax.numpy.

from jax import grad,jit
def sigmoid(x):
    return 1 / (1 + jnp.exp(-x))
def predict(x, w1,b1,w2,b2):
    z = sigmoid(jnp.dot(x, w1)+b1)
    return sigmoid(jnp.dot(z, w2)+b2)[:,0]
def nll(x, y, w1,b1,w2,b2):
    yhat = predict(x, w1,b1,w2,b2)
    return -jnp.sum(y * jnp.log(yhat) + (1 - y) * jnp.log(1 - yhat))
@jit
def gd_step(x, y, w1,b1,w2,b2, lr):
    grads = grad(nll,argnums=[2,3,4,5])(x, y, w1,b1,w2,b2)
    return w1 - lr * grads[0],b1 - lr * grads[1],w2 - lr * grads[2],b2 - lr * grads[3]
def accuracy(x, y, w1,b1,w2,b2):
    y_pred = predict(x, w1,b1,w2,b2)
    return jnp.mean((y_pred > 0.5) == y)


for i in range(1500):
    w1,b1,w2,b2 = gd_step(x,y,w1,b1,w2,b2,0.02)
print(accuracy(x,y,w1,b1,w2,b2))
## 1.0

Note that inside the gradient descent function gd_step we use the grad function to calculate the gradient of the negative log-likelihood function with respect to the weights and biases. The jit decorator is used to compile the function for faster execution. The gd_step function updates the weights and biases using the calculated gradients and a learning rate of 0.02. The printed number is the accuracy on the training data.
Finally, we can plot the data with the line each of the four hidden units draws in the input space









We can see that the model has learned to separate the two classes. Two of the lines, the two nearly parallel ones at the upper right, both cut off the same side of the cluster, so those two hidden units do largely the same job. We could have gotten away with using only three hidden units instead of four.

title: 20  Gradient Descent
text:
20.4 Advanced Optimization Methods
While the basic SGD algorithm introduced earlier works well for many problems, practitioners have developed numerous enhancements to improve convergence speed and stability.

Momentum Methods
One limitation of vanilla SGD is that the descent in the loss function is not guaranteed at every iteration, and progress can be slow when gradients are noisy. To address this, momentum-based methods add memory to the search process by combining new gradient information with previous search directions (Polyak 1964). Empirically, momentum-based methods have been shown to have better convergence for deep learning networks (Sutskever et al. 2013). The gradient only influences changes in the velocity of the update, which then updates the variable. Below \(g\) is the mini-batch gradient of the loss, \(k\) the iteration, \(t_k\) the learning rate (the \(\alpha_t\) above), \((W,b)\) the weights and biases, and squares and roots of vectors are taken elementwise:
\[
v^{k+1} = \mu v^k - t_k g((W,b)^k)
\] \[
(W,b)^{k+1} = (W,b)^k + v^{k+1}
\]
The hyperparameter \(\mu\) controls the damping effect on the rate of update of the variables. The physical analogy is the reduction in kinetic energy that allows us to “slow down” the movements at the minima. This parameter can also be chosen empirically using cross-validation.
Nesterov’s momentum method (Nesterov 1983) (a.k.a. Nesterov acceleration) calculates the gradient at the point predicted by the momentum. One can view this as a look-ahead strategy with the updating scheme
\[
v^{k+1} = \mu v^k - t_k g((W,b)^k + \mu v^k)
\] \[
(W,b)^{k+1} = (W,b)^k + v^{k+1}
\]


Adaptive Learning Rate Methods
Another popular modification is AdaGrad (Duchi, Hazan, and Singer 2011), which adaptively scales the learning rate for each parameter based on the history of gradients:
\[
c^{k+1} = c^k + g(\theta^k)^2
\] \[
\theta^{k+1} = \theta^k - \frac{t_k}{\sqrt{c^{k+1}} + \epsilon} g(\theta^k)
\]
where \(\epsilon\) is a small constant (e.g., \(\epsilon = 10^{-8}\)) to prevent division by zero. RMSprop (Hinton, Srivastava, and Swersky 2012) extends AdaGrad by using an exponentially weighted moving average of squared gradients:
\[
c^{k+1} = \rho c^k + (1-\rho) g(\theta^k)^2
\] \[
\theta^{k+1} = \theta^k - \frac{t_k}{\sqrt{c^{k+1}} + \epsilon} g(\theta^k)
\]
The Adam method (Kingma and Ba 2014) combines RMSprop with momentum by maintaining exponentially weighted averages of both the gradient (first moment) and the squared gradient (second moment):
\[
m^{k+1} = \beta_1 m^k + (1-\beta_1) g(\theta^k)
\] \[
c^{k+1} = \beta_2 c^k + (1-\beta_2) g(\theta^k)^2
\] \[
\theta^{k+1} = \theta^k - \frac{t_k}{\sqrt{\hat{c}^{k+1}} + \epsilon} \hat{m}^{k+1}
\]
where \(\hat{m}^{k+1} = m^{k+1}/(1-\beta_1^{k+1})\) and \(\hat{c}^{k+1} = c^{k+1}/(1-\beta_2^{k+1})\) are bias-corrected estimates, with \(m^0 = c^0 = 0\). The typical hyperparameter values are \(\beta_1 = 0.9\), \(\beta_2 = 0.999\), and \(\epsilon = 10^{-8}\).








Method
Key Idea
Update Rule




SGD

\(\theta^{k+1} = \theta^k - t_k g^k\)

\(v^{k+1} = \mu v^k - t_k g^k\); \(\theta^{k+1} = \theta^k + v^{k+1}\)

\(v^{k+1} = \mu v^k - t_k g(\theta^k + \mu v^k)\); \(\theta^{k+1} = \theta^k + v^{k+1}\)

Second-Order Methods
Second-order methods solve the optimization problem by solving a system of nonlinear equations \(\nabla f(\theta) = 0\) using Newton’s method:
\[
\theta^{+} = \theta - \{ \nabla^2 f(\theta) \}^{-1} \nabla f(\theta)
\]
We can see that SGD effectively approximates the inverse Hessian \(\{\nabla^2 f(\theta)\}^{-1}\) by \(t_k I\), where \(I\) is the identity matrix. The advantages of second-order methods include much faster convergence rates and insensitivity to the conditioning of the problem. However, in practice, second-order methods are rarely used for deep learning applications (Dean et al. 2012). Since typical deep learning models rely on large-scale datasets, computing and storing the Hessian becomes memory and computationally prohibitive.

title: 20  Gradient Descent
text:
20.5 Why Robbins-Monro?
The Robbins-Monro algorithm was introduced in their seminal 1951 paper “A Stochastic Approximation Method” Robbins and Monro (1951). The paper addressed the problem of finding the root of a function when only noisy observations are available.
Consider a function \(M(\theta)\) where we want to find \(\theta^*\) such that \(M(\theta^*) = \alpha\) for some target value \(\alpha\). In the original formulation, \(M(\theta)\) represents the expected value of some random variable \(Y(\theta)\):
\[M(\theta) = \E{Y(\theta)} = \alpha\]
The key insight is that we can only observe noisy realizations \(y(\theta)\) where:
\[y(\theta) = M(\theta) + \epsilon(\theta)\]
where \(\epsilon(\theta)\) is a zero-mean random error term.
The Robbins-Monro algorithm iteratively updates the estimate \(\theta_n\) using:
\[\theta_{n+1} = \theta_n - a_n(y(\theta_n) - \alpha)\]
where \(a_n\) is a sequence of positive step sizes that must satisfy:
\[\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n = \infty \quad \text{and} \quad \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n^2 < \infty\]
These conditions ensure that the algorithm can explore the entire space (first condition) while eventually converging (second condition).
Under appropriate conditions on \(M(\theta)\) (monotonicity and boundedness), the algorithm converges in mean square (Robbins and Monro 1951) and almost surely (Blum 1954) to \(\theta^*\):
\[\lim_{n \to \infty} \theta_n = \theta^* \quad \text{almost surely}\]
The convergence rate depends on the choice of step sizes. For \(a_n = c/n\) with \(c > 0\) and \(c\) sufficiently large, the mean squared error \(\E{(\theta_n - \theta^*)^2}\) decreases as \(O(1/n)\) (Chung 1954).
This foundational work established the theoretical basis for stochastic approximation methods that are now widely used in machine learning, particularly in stochastic gradient descent and related optimization algorithms.

Connection to M-Estimation
The Robbins-Monro framework connects naturally to statistical estimation. Many estimands, including means, medians, quantiles, and regression coefficients, can be expressed as solutions to convex optimization problems:
\[\theta^* = \arg\min_{\theta \in \mathbb{R}^p} \E{\rho_\theta(X_i, Y_i)},\]
where \(\rho_\theta\) is a convex loss function. Under mild conditions, the optimum \(\theta^*\) satisfies the first-order condition: \[
\E{g_\theta(X_i, Y_i)} = 0,
\tag{20.1}\]
where \(g_\theta\) is a subgradient of the loss. SGD can be viewed as applying the Robbins-Monro algorithm to find roots of this gradient condition using noisy samples.

title: 20  Gradient Descent
section: 20.6 The EM, ECM, and ECME Algorithms
text:
20.6 The EM, ECM, and ECME Algorithms
Gradient descent is not the only iterative optimization algorithm used in statistics. When dealing with latent variables or missing data, directly computing gradients of the log-likelihood can be intractable. The Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm provides an elegant alternative that iteratively maximizes a surrogate function, avoiding explicit gradient computation while guaranteeing monotonic improvement in the likelihood.
First, define a function \(B(\theta,\phi)\) that minorizes the objective \(\ell(\theta)\) at \(\phi\), that is, \(B(\theta,\phi) \leq \ell(\theta)\) for all \(\theta\) and \(B(\phi,\phi) = \ell(\phi)\). Then define
\[\theta^{(g+1)} = \arg\max_{\theta \in \Theta} B(\theta,\theta^{(g)})\]
Maximizing \(B(\theta,\theta^{(g)})\) over \(\theta\) guarantees monotone improvement. To see this, we get a sequence of inequalities
\[\ell(\theta^{(0)}) = B(\theta^{(0)},\theta^{(0)}) \leq B(\theta^{(1)},\theta^{(0)}) \leq \ell(\theta^{(1)}) = B(\theta^{(1)},\theta^{(1)}) \leq \ldots\]
so \(\ell(\theta^{(g)})\) is non-decreasing and, when \(\ell\) is bounded above, converges.
In many models we have to deal with a latent variable and require estimation where integration is also involved. For example, suppose that we have a triple \((y,z,\theta)\) with joint probability specification \(p(y,z,\theta) = p(y\mid z,\theta)p(z,\theta)\). This can occur in missing data problems and estimation problems in mixture models.
A standard application of the EM algorithm is to find
\[\arg\max_{\theta \in \Theta} \int_z p(y\mid z,\theta)p(z\mid\theta)dz\]
As we are just finding an optimum, we do not need the prior specification \(p(\theta)\). The EM algorithm finds a sequence of parameter values \(\theta^{(g)}\) by alternating between an expectation and a maximization step. This still requires the numerical (or analytical) computation of the criterion function \(Q(\theta,\theta^{(g)})\) described below.
EM algorithms have been used extensively in mixture models and missing data problems. The EM algorithm uses the particular choice where
\[\ell(\theta) = \log p(y\mid\theta) = \log \int p(y,z\mid\theta)dz\]
Here the likelihood has a mixture representation where \(z\) is the latent variable (missing data, state variable, etc.). This is termed a Q-maximization algorithm with:
\[Q(\theta,\theta^{(g)}) = \int \log p(y,z\mid\theta)p(z\mid\theta^{(g)},y)dz = \E[z\mid\theta^{(g)},y]{\log p(y,z\mid\theta)}\]
The function \(B(\theta,\phi) = Q(\theta,\phi) + H(\phi)\), with \(H(\phi) = -\E[z\mid\phi,y]{\log p(z\mid y,\phi)}\) free of \(\theta\), minorizes \(\ell\) at \(\phi\): \(B(\theta,\phi) \leq \ell(\theta)\) by Gibbs’ inequality, with equality at \(\theta = \phi\). Maximizing \(Q\) over \(\theta\) therefore maximizes \(B\).
To implement EM you need to be able to calculate \(Q(\theta,\theta^{(g)})\) and optimize at each iteration.
The EM algorithm and its extensions ECM and ECME are methods of computing maximum likelihood estimates or posterior modes in the presence of missing data. Let the objective function be \(\ell(\theta) = \log p(\theta\mid y) + c(y)\), where \(c(y)\) is a possibly unknown normalizing constant that does not depend on \(\theta\), and \(y\) denotes observed data. We have a mixture representation,
\[p(\theta\mid y) = \int p(\theta,z\mid y)dz = \int p(\theta\mid z,y)p(z\mid y)dz\]
where distribution of the latent variables is \(p(z\mid\theta,y) = p(y\mid\theta,z)p(z\mid\theta)/p(y\mid\theta)\).
In some cases, the complete data log-posterior is simple enough for \(\arg\max_{\theta} \log p(\theta\mid z,y)\) to be computed in closed form. The EM algorithm alternates between the Expectation and Maximization steps for which it is named. The E-step and M-step computes
\[Q(\theta,\theta^{(g)}) = \E[z\mid\theta^{(g)},y]{\log p(\theta\mid z,y)} = \int \log p(\theta\mid z,y)p(z\mid\theta^{(g)},y)dz\]
\[\theta^{(g+1)} = \arg\max_{\theta} Q(\theta,\theta^{(g)})\]
This has an important monotonicity property that ensures \(\ell(\theta^{(g)}) \leq \ell(\theta^{(g+1)})\) for all \(g\). In fact, the monotonicity proof given by Dempster, Laird, and Rubin (1977) shows that any \(\theta\) with \(Q(\theta,\theta^{(g)}) \geq Q(\theta^{(g)},\theta^{(g)})\) also satisfies the inequality \(\ell(\theta) \geq \ell(\theta^{(g)})\).
In problems with many parameters, the M-step of EM may be difficult. In this case \(\theta\) may be partitioned into components \((\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_k)\) in such a way that maximizing \(\log p(\theta_j\mid\theta_{-j},z,y)\) is easy. The ECM algorithm (Meng and Rubin 1993) pairs the EM algorithm’s E-step with \(k\) conditional maximization (CM) steps, each maximizing \(Q\) over one component \(\theta_j\) with each component of \(\theta_{-j}\) fixed at the most recent value. Due to the fact that each CM step increases \(Q\), the ECM algorithm retains the monotonicity property. The ECME algorithm replaces some of ECM’s CM steps with maximizations over \(\ell\) instead of \(Q\). Liu and Rubin (1994) show that doing so can greatly increase the rate of convergence.
Seen through the optimization lens, ECM is a form of block coordinate ascent on a surrogate objective: it improves parameters one block at a time while holding the rest fixed. This contrasts with SGD, which takes small stochastic steps along noisy gradients of a single objective; both are iterative methods, but they trade off different sources of computational convenience (closed-form block updates versus cheap gradient estimates).
In many cases we will have a parameter vector \(\theta = (\beta,\nu)\) partitioned into its components and a missing data vector \(z = (\lambda,\omega)\). Then we compute the \(Q(\beta,\nu\mid\beta^{(g)},\nu^{(g)})\) objective function and then compute E- and M steps from this to provide an iterative algorithm for updating parameters. To update the hyperparameter \(\nu\) we can maximize the observed-data posterior \(p(\beta,\nu\mid y)\) with \(\beta\) fixed at \(\beta^{(g+1)}\). The algorithm can be summarized as follows:
\[\beta^{(g+1)} = \arg\max_{\beta} Q(\beta\mid\beta^{(g)},\nu^{(g)}) \quad \text{where} \quad Q(\beta\mid\beta^{(g)},\nu^{(g)}) = \E[z\mid\beta^{(g)},\nu^{(g)},y]{\log p(\beta\mid\nu^{(g)},z,y)}\]
\[\nu^{(g+1)} = \arg\max_{\nu} \log p(\beta^{(g+1)},\nu\mid y)\]

Example 20.3 (Simulated Annealing) Simulated Annealing (SA) (Kirkpatrick, Gelatt, and Vecchi 1983) is a simulation-based approach to finding
\[\hat{\theta} = \arg\max_{\theta \in \Theta} H(\theta)\]
\[\pi_J(\theta) = \frac{e^{JH(\theta)}}{\int e^{JH(\theta)}d\mu(\theta)}\]
where \(J\) is an inverse temperature parameter. Instead of looking at derivatives and performing gradient-based optimization, you can simulate from the sequence of densities. This forms a time-inhomogeneous Markov chain, and under suitable regularity conditions on the relaxation schedule for the temperature we have \(\theta^{(g)} \to \hat{\theta}\). The main caveat is that we need to know the criterion function \(H(\theta)\) to evaluate the Metropolis probability for sampling from the sequence of densities. This is not always available.
An interesting generalization which is appropriate in latent variable mixture models is the following. Suppose that \(H(\theta) = \E[z\mid\theta]{H(z,\theta)}\) is unavailable in closed-form where we assume that \(H(z,\theta) \geq 0\) (if \(H\) is bounded below, add a constant). In this case, we can use latent variable simulated annealing (LVSA) methods. Define a joint probability distribution for \(z_J = (z_1,\ldots,z_J)\) as
\[\pi_J(z_J,\theta) \propto \prod_{j=1}^J H(z_j,\theta)p(z_j\mid\theta)\mu(\theta)\]
for some measure \(\mu\) which ensures integrability of the joint. This distribution has the property that its marginal distribution on \(\theta\) is given by
\[\pi_J(\theta) \propto \E[z\mid\theta]{H(z,\theta)}^J \mu(\theta) = e^{J \log H(\theta)}\mu(\theta)\]
By the simulated annealing argument we see that this marginal collapses on the maximum of \(\log H(\theta)\). The advantage of this approach is that it is typically straightforward to sample with MCMC from the conditionals:
\[\pi_J(z_j\mid\theta) \propto H(z_j,\theta)p(z_j\mid\theta) \quad \text{and} \quad \pi_J(\theta\mid z_J) \propto \prod_{j=1}^J H(z_j,\theta)p(z_j\mid\theta)\mu(\theta)\]
Jacquier, Johannes, and Polson (2007) apply this framework to finding MLE estimates for commonly encountered latent variable models. The LVSA approach is particularly useful when the criterion function involves complex integrals that make direct optimization challenging, but where sampling from the conditional distributions remains tractable.

title: 20  Gradient Descent
text:
20.7 Conclusion
This chapter has covered the computational foundations of training deep learning models. Several key insights emerge:
Gradient Descent as the Foundation: While classical statistical methods rely on second-order optimization (Newton-Raphson, BFGS), deep learning’s scale demands first-order methods. Gradient descent, despite its simplicity, remains effective because it requires only gradient information, which scales linearly with the number of parameters.
Stochastic Approximation: The Robbins-Monro framework provides theoretical justification for SGD: noisy gradient estimates, when properly scheduled, converge to the optimum of a convex problem. Mini-batch SGD exploits this insight, trading exact gradients for computational efficiency and, counterintuitively, often better generalization (Keskar et al. 2016).
Automatic Differentiation: The backpropagation algorithm is simply reverse-mode automatic differentiation applied to neural networks. Understanding this connection reveals why modern frameworks (PyTorch, JAX) can automatically compute gradients for arbitrary computational graphs. The key insight is that reverse mode is efficient when outputs are few and parameters are many, precisely the situation in supervised learning.
Advanced Optimizers: Building on vanilla SGD, momentum methods accelerate convergence by accumulating gradient information, while adaptive methods (AdaGrad, RMSprop, Adam) automatically tune per-parameter learning rates. These innovations are widely used to train deep networks efficiently, though the optimal choice remains problem-dependent.
Beyond Gradients: The EM algorithm provides an alternative optimization paradigm for latent variable models, avoiding explicit gradient computation. Simulated annealing offers yet another approach, using stochastic sampling to escape local minima.
The practical success of SGD and its variants remains somewhat surprising from a theoretical perspective. Why does an algorithm analyzed for convex optimization work so well on highly non-convex loss landscapes? Ongoing research suggests that the geometry of over-parameterized networks may be more benign than previously thought: saddle points abound (Dauphin et al. 2014), but local minima tend to generalize well. Understanding these phenomena remains an active area of research at the intersection of optimization theory and deep learning.

Exercise 20.3 (Newton’s Method versus Gradient Descent) Consider the quadratic objective \[
f(x) = \frac{1}{2} x^\top A x - b^\top x, \qquad x \in \mathbb{R}^d,
\] where \(A\) is a symmetric positive definite \(d \times d\) matrix and \(b \in \mathbb{R}^d\). Newton’s method uses curvature information to take more efficient steps than gradient descent, so why does deep learning rely on first-order methods instead, as the Second-Order Methods section of this chapter explains?

Derive the gradient \(\nabla f(x)\) and the Hessian \(\nabla^2 f(x)\).
Write the gradient descent update with fixed step size \(\alpha\), and the Newton update \(x^{t+1} = x^t - \{\nabla^2 f(x^t)\}^{-1} \nabla f(x^t)\), both specialized to this \(f\).
Show algebraically that, starting from any \(x^0\), Newton’s method reaches the minimizer \(x^* = A^{-1}b\) in exactly one step. Explain why this does not happen for gradient descent, and why the one-step argument does not carry over to a non-quadratic objective.
For gradient descent with fixed step size \(\alpha\), state a condition on \(\alpha\) relative to the eigenvalues of \(A\) that guarantees convergence.
Newton’s method looks strictly better after part (c). Explain why it is nonetheless impractical for deep learning models with \(d\) in the millions or billions: compare the storage cost of the Hessian (\(O(d^2)\) entries) to that of the gradient (\(O(d)\) entries), and the cost of solving the Newton system (equivalently, factoring the Hessian, \(O(d^3)\) by standard methods such as Cholesky or LU decomposition) to the cost of one gradient step (\(O(d)\) via a single backpropagation pass, as in the Automatic Differentiation section of this chapter).
Illustrate parts (c)-(e) numerically in R for a small example.



Exercise 20.4 (Robbins-Monro Step-Size Conditions) The Why Robbins-Monro? section states that the recursion \(\theta_{n+1} = \theta_n - a_n\,(y(\theta_n) - \alpha)\) converges almost surely to the root \(\theta^*\) provided the positive step sizes satisfy the two summability conditions \[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n = \infty
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n^2 < \infty .
\] The first condition guarantees the iterates can travel far enough to reach \(\theta^*\) from any starting point; the second forces the steps to shrink fast enough that the observation noise averages out. This exercise pins down which schedules satisfy them and shows what breaks when they do not.

For the power-law family \(a_n = c/n^p\) with \(c > 0\) and \(p > 0\), use the \(p\)-series test to find the exact range of \(p\) for which both conditions hold. Does the constant \(c\) affect the answer?
Classify the schedules \(a_n = c\) (constant, \(p = 0\)), \(a_n = c/\sqrt{n}\) (\(p = 1/2\)), \(a_n = c/n^{0.9}\) (\(p = 0.9\)), \(a_n = c/n\) (\(p = 1\)), and \(a_n = c/n^2\) (\(p = 2\)) against your answer to (a). For each schedule that fails a condition, state which one fails and give a one-sentence description of what goes wrong in the algorithm.
In Python, verify the classification numerically by computing the partial sums \(\sum_{n=1}^{N} a_n\) and \(\sum_{n=1}^{N} a_n^2\) (with \(c = 1\)) up to \(N = 10^6\) for the five schedules. The stall predicted for a too-fast schedule (\(p > 1\)) needs a problem whose gradient stays bounded. title: 21  Quantile Neural Networks
text:
21.1 Quantile Regression
With the architecture (Chapter 18) and training algorithms (Chapter 20) of neural networks in hand, we now apply them to a problem at the intersection of Bayesian inference and decision theory.
In Chapter 3, we explored how to learn posterior distributions \(p(\theta\mid y)\) using Bayesian learning and to use it for predictions, hypothesis testing, and other tasks. In Chapter 4, we explored how rational agents make decisions under uncertainty by maximizing expected utility. Traditional Bayesian approaches to such problems require computing posterior distributions \(p(\theta\mid y)\), which in turn requires specifying likelihood functions \(p(y\mid \theta)\) and often involves challenging posterior estimation.1 But what if we could bypass density estimation entirely and directly learn the quantities we need for decision-making and other tasks?
This chapter introduces quantile neural networks, which learn posterior distributions through their quantile functions rather than their densities. This shift from densities to quantiles enables likelihood-free inference, provides direct connections to decision theory through the quantile-expectation identity, and scales to high-dimensional problems where density estimation becomes intractable.
The key insight is straightforward. Any expectation, including the expected utility central to decision theory, can be represented as an integral over quantiles: \[
\E{f(\theta)\mid y} = \int_0^1 F^{-1}_{f(\theta) \mid y}(\tau) d\tau
\] Rather than learning densities and then computing expectations via sampling, we can directly learn the quantile function \(F^{-1}_{f(\theta) \mid y}(\tau)\) using neural networks. This approach is not only more efficient but also naturally handles simulation-based models where likelihoods are unavailable or computationally expensive.2
We begin with quantile regression (Section 21.1) and neural network implementation (Section 21.2), then use demand forecasts for an inventory decision. Posterior and utility quantiles extend the same learning objective to Bayesian inference and decision theory. Quantile trend filtering and distributional reinforcement learning follow as further comparisons.
A retailer must choose tomorrow’s stock before observing demand \(D\). Under a single-period model with no fixed ordering cost or capacity constraint, let \(c_u\) be the cost per unit of unmet demand and \(c_o\) the cost per unit left over. Writing \(v^+ = \max(v,0)\), the expected cost is \[
C(q) = \E{c_u(D-q)^+ + c_o(q-D)^+} = (c_u+c_o)\E{\rho_\tau(D-q)}, \qquad \tau = \frac{c_u}{c_u+c_o}.
\] Here \(\rho_\tau\) is the check loss defined below. If a shortage costs nine times as much as a leftover, the optimal stock level is the 90th percentile of demand. The asymmetric costs determine the statistical target.
For observed values \(y_1, \ldots, y_n\), a sample median minimizes the sum of absolute deviations: \[
m \in \arg\min_q \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n |y_i-q|.
\] A population median similarly minimizes \(\E{|Y-q|}\), assuming a finite first moment. At least half the probability lies on each side of a median.
The median is the special case \(\tau = 0.5\), but the same principle generalizes to any quantile \(\tau \in (0,1)\). We use a generalization of the absolute value function, the check loss or pinball loss (Koenker and Bassett 1978), to find the minimizer: \[
q_\tau = \arg\min_q \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \rho_\tau(y_i - q).
\] Here \(\rho_\tau(u)\) is the check loss, defined as: \[
\rho_\tau(u) = u(\tau - I(u < 0)) = \begin{cases}
\tau u & \text{if } u \geq 0 \\
(\tau - 1) u & \text{if } u < 0
\end{cases}
\] For a continuous conditional distribution, differentiating the population risk gives \[
\frac{\partial}{\partial q} \E{\rho_\tau(Y-q)\mid X=x} = F_{Y\mid X=x}(q)-\tau.
\] The derivative is negative below the requested quantile and positive above it. For discrete demand, the corresponding subgradient condition is \(F(q^-)\leq\tau\leq F(q)\). Thus minimizing check loss selects a conditional quantile, including the stock level required by the cost ratio.
Linear quantile regression restricts each quantile to a linear predictor. Neural quantile regression replaces that predictor with a learned nonlinear function and can share features across quantiles. The loss continues to identify the same statistical target.

title: 21  Quantile Neural Networks
text:
Example 21.1 (Linear Quantile Regression) To illustrate quantile regression, we analyze engine displacement and fuel efficiency in mtcars. Alongside the mean relationship from ordinary least squares, we estimate conditional quantiles on the log-log scale (Figure 21.1).

# Define the check loss (pinball loss) function
check_loss <- function(u, tau) {
    # rho_tau(u) = u * (tau - I(u < 0))
    u * (tau - (u < 0))
}

# Objective function: sum of check losses for quantile regression
quantile_objective <- function(beta, X, y, tau) {
    y_pred <- X %*% beta
    residuals <- y - y_pred
    sum(check_loss(residuals, tau))
}

# Prepare data
X <- cbind(1, log(mtcars$disp)) # Design matrix with intercept
y <- log(mtcars$mpg)

We minimize this objective with optim (BFGS, started at the least squares fit) separately for \(\tau = 0.1, 0.5, 0.9\), and compare the three fitted lines with ordinary least squares on the log-log scale.

Table 21.1 shows the estimated coefficients.

The slopes differ across quantiles: the 10th percentile slope is -0.5340, while the 90th percentile slope is -0.3660. The fitted negative relationship is stronger at the lower quantile, so the gap between the fitted quantiles widens with displacement. These data do not identify the causes of that spread.
Unlike squared-error loss, absolute loss does not give increasingly large residuals increasingly large slopes. Median regression is therefore less sensitive to extreme response values than OLS, although unusual predictor values can still have substantial influence.
Finally, the check loss \(\rho_\tau(u)\) is piecewise linear, making it non-differentiable at zero. BFGS assumes a smooth objective, so it is not guaranteed to reach the minimum here, and in this example optim stops slightly short of it: the slopes are within 0.01 of those of the linear programming algorithm of quantreg::rq, the standard way to fit quantile regression (Koenker 2005).

title: 21  Quantile Neural Networks
text:
21.2 Neural Network Implementation
A conditional quantile network \(q_{\varphi}(x,\tau)\) receives the observed features \(x\) and a quantile level \(\tau\in(0,1)\), and predicts \(F^{-1}_{Y\mid X=x}(\tau)\). Here \(\varphi\) denotes network weights, distinct from Bayesian model parameters \(\theta\). Given training pairs \((x_i,y_i)\) and levels \(\tau_1,\ldots,\tau_K\), minimize pure averaged pinball loss: \[
L(\varphi) = \frac{1}{NK}\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{k=1}^K \rho_{\tau_k}\big(y_i-q_{\varphi}(x_i,\tau_k)\big).
\] Alternatively, draw independent uniform levels during training. At each fixed \((x,\tau)\), the population loss is minimized by the conditional quantile, as the derivative above shows. An independently drawn \(\tau\) specifies which quantile to estimate; it does not turn an observed \(y_i\) into that quantile.
A mini-batch update makes the learning mechanism explicit. Sample a batch \(B\) of observed pairs and draw \(\tau_i\sim U(0,1)\) independently for each pair. With step size \(\eta\), take a stochastic subgradient update: \[
\varphi \leftarrow \varphi-\eta\,\partial_{\varphi}\left[\frac{1}{|B|}\sum_{i\in B}\rho_{\tau_i}\big(y_i-q_{\varphi}(x_i,\tau_i)\big)\right].
\] No MSE term is needed to identify quantiles. Adding squared error to the same output generally shifts its population minimizer away from the requested quantile; a conditional median need not equal a conditional mean. A separate mean output could share features, but would estimate a different target.
Rather than training separate networks for each \(\tau_k\), one network takes \(\tau\) as an input and shares features across levels. It can also be evaluated at untrained levels. Neither sharing nor interpolation guarantees accuracy or prevents quantile crossing.

Cosine Embedding for \(\tau\)
One architectural choice is to concatenate \(\tau\) with the other inputs. Another is a cosine embedding, used by Dabney et al. (2018): \[
F^{-1}(\tau,x) \approx q_{\varphi}(x,\tau) = g(\psi(x)\circ\phi(\tau)),
\] where \(\circ\) is element-wise multiplication, \(g\) and \(\psi\) are feed-forward networks, and \[
\phi_j(\tau) = \mathrm{ReLU}\left(\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\cos(\pi i\tau)w_{ij}+b_j\right), \qquad j=1,\ldots,m.
\] The scalar \(\tau\) becomes an \(m\)-dimensional vector using \(n\) cosine frequencies. This branch depends only on \(\tau\); the feature branch \(\psi(x)\) supplies the conditioning information. Sharing these branches across quantiles can reduce parameter counts relative to separate networks.
The cosine basis motivates the embedding, but does not guarantee smooth or monotone quantiles. Discrete outcomes can have discontinuous quantile functions, and ReLU introduces kinks. Barron (1993) gives \(O(N^{-1/2})\) approximation rates for networks with \(N\) sigmoidal units under a finite first Fourier-moment condition; that result is not a rate for this cosine embedding.


Non-Crossing Constraints
A valid quantile function satisfies \(F^{-1}(\tau_i)\leq F^{-1}(\tau_j)\) when \(\tau_i<\tau_j\). Unconstrained networks can violate this ordering. Remedies include penalties on crossings, architectures constrained to be non-decreasing in \(\tau\), and rearrangement of predictions after fitting (Chernozhukov, Fernández-Val, and Galichon 2010; Cannon 2018). Monotone activation functions alone do not guarantee a monotone network: the weights and how \(\tau\) enters must also be constrained.
These are possible safeguards, rather than procedures used by every example below. The reproducible neural comparison uses no crossing penalty or rearrangement, so ordering must be checked separately.


Synthetic Data Example
Consider synthetic data generated from the model: \[
x\sim U(-1,1),\qquad y\mid x\sim N\left(\frac{\sin(\pi x)}{\pi x},\frac{\exp(1-x)}{10}\right).
\] The variance increases as \(x\) decreases. Write \(\operatorname{sinc}(x)=\sin(\pi x)/(\pi x)\), with \(\operatorname{sinc}(0)=1\) by continuity. The true conditional quantile is \[
f_\tau(x)=\operatorname{sinc}(x)+\Phi^{-1}(\tau)\sqrt{\frac{\exp(1-x)}{10}}.
\] An implicit network learns a function of both \(x\) and \(\tau\). An explicit approach fits separate outputs at selected levels, illustrated here at \(\tau\in\{0.05,0.5,0.95\}\).






Figure 21.2: Illustration of quantile predictions for the synthetic model. The outer levels, 0.05 and 0.95, define a nominal 90% prediction interval. Visual agreement with the true curves does not measure achieved coverage.



For an inspectable comparison on the same model, the computing exercise “Cosine Embeddings for the Quantile Level” supplies the full training code (the computing exercises appear in the HTML edition and in the notebooks of exercises/). It generates 400 pairs with seed 7. The implicit network has eight cosine frequencies, embedding dimension six, a \(1\to6\) tanh feature network, and a linear readout. Nine explicit networks each use a \(1\to6\) tanh feature layer and linear readout. Both minimize summed pinball loss at \(\tau=0.1,0.2,\ldots,0.9\) using optim with L-BFGS-B and maxit = 300; the explicit initializations use seed 11. Quantile levels are fixed in this comparison, rather than sampled randomly.



Table 21.2: Mean absolute quantile error at \(\tau=0.37\) from the reproducible exercise, evaluated against the known quantile on \(x\in\{-0.9,-0.7,\ldots,0.9\}\).

The implicit network answers directly at the untrained level 0.37; the explicit approach linearly interpolates its 0.3 and 0.4 fits. The errors in Table 21.2 are similar, with the explicit interpolation slightly better in this run. Sharing uses fewer parameters here, but establishes neither an accuracy advantage nor calibration across all levels. This experiment is separate from the illustration in Figure 21.2.


Quantiles and Wasserstein Distance
For scalar distributions with finite first moments, the 1-Wasserstein distance is \[
W_1(P_U,P_V)=\int_0^1\left|F_U^{-1}(\tau)-F_V^{-1}(\tau)\right|d\tau.
\] It can be computed from order statistics (Levina and Bickel 2001). Matching every target quantile makes this distance zero. This is the population-target connection used in Exercise 21.4, rather than an identity between empirical pinball loss and \(W_1\). In a restricted neural family, minimizing one need not minimize the other. For an equal-weight approximation by \(K\) point masses, the \(W_1\)-optimal locations are the target quantiles at \((2k-1)/(2K)\), \(k=1,\ldots,K\) (Dabney et al. 2017).
Wasserstein GANs use this distributional distance because it can distinguish disjoint supports (Arjovsky, Chintala, and Bottou 2017). That motivation does not make arbitrary quantile-network training equivalent to GAN training or guarantee its stability.

title: 21  Quantile Neural Networks
text:
21.3 Supply Chain Forecasting at Scale
Large retailers must choose stock levels for many products and locations. Too little inventory leads to stockouts and lost sales; too much ties up capital and risks obsolescence. We return to the asymmetric inventory choice that motivated check loss.
For the single-period costs defined in Section 21.1, the optimal stock target is \(F^{-1}_{D\mid x}(c_u/(c_u+c_o))\). Here \(P_k\) (written Pk in the figures) is the \(k\)th percentile of demand. P50 is optimal only when the unit costs are equal. P90 corresponds to a shortage cost nine times the overage cost; it is a demand level, whereas safety stock usually means inventory above an expected-demand baseline over a specified replenishment period. Capacity planning can also use a high quantile, with the level determined by the relevant costs or service constraint.
For a high-margin item with \(c_u/c_o\) between \(7/3\) and \(4\), the optimal policy may target \(P_{70}\) or \(P_{80}\). For perishable goods with \(c_u/c_o\) between \(3/7\) and \(2/3\), target \(P_{30}\) or \(P_{40}\). These are cost-based examples, not fixed rules for product categories (Exercise 21.6).
DeepAR (Salinas, Flunkert, and Gasthaus 2019) is a recurrent probabilistic forecasting model that predicts parameters of a chosen distribution, such as a Gaussian or negative binomial, from related time series. Quantiles can be obtained analytically where available or by sampling. The multi-horizon quantile recurrent forecaster of Wen et al. (2017) directly predicts demand quantiles at several horizons using check loss. Chronos-2 (Ansari et al. 2025) extends pretrained forecasting to univariate, multivariate, and covariate-informed tasks.
Direct quantile prediction accommodates asymmetric costs without choosing a parametric response family. It can represent zero-demand quantiles, although intermittent demand still requires adequate data and a suitable model. Linear growth of the loss limits the influence of extreme response residuals; promotional effects still need predictors. Feature choices and network restrictions remain modeling assumptions.

Demand Forecasting Setup
Consider forecasting demand \(y_t\) for a product given the features in Table 21.3:



Table 21.3: Features for demand forecasting.










Feature Category
Examples
Purpose

Day of week, month, holiday indicators, days since launch
Capture seasonal patterns and product lifecycle


Lagged demand
\(y_{t-1}, y_{t-7}, y_{t-28}\) (yesterday, last week, last month)
Incorporate recent demand history and autocorrelation

Account for product-specific characteristics

Weather, events, competitor prices

The model predicts conditional quantiles: \[
q_\tau(t) = F^{-1}_{Y_t \mid X_t}(\tau)
\]
where \(X_t\) contains information available when the forecast is issued. Training pairs \((y_t,x_t)\) may be pooled across products.


A Possible Neural Architecture
Product embeddings can share information across related items, while recurrent or attention layers encode history and its interactions with numerical features. Such sharing may help products with little history when their relationships transfer. One possible architecture uses the same two branches as Section 21.2.






Figure 21.3: A possible demand quantile architecture. Product embeddings, encoded sales history and numeric features are fused into \(h_t\); an independent branch embeds the requested quantile level \(\tau\), and the quantile head combines the two.



In Figure 21.3, the branch \(\phi(\tau)\), a cosine embedding as in Section 21.2, receives only \(\tau\), independently of feature fusion. Training can sample products and historical forecast origins in mini-batches and minimize averaged pinball loss.


An Instructional Linear Baseline
The following simulation uses three products over two years. It includes positive trends, weekly and monthly seasonality, promotions on approximately 10% of days, and noise whose standard deviation grows with demand. The promotional increments range from 50 to 90 units. These patterns are stipulated by the simulator.
Five linear quantile regressions are fitted separately at \(\tau\in\{0.1,0.3,0.5,0.7,0.9\}\), using product identifier, day, promotion, numerical day-of-week and day-of-month features, and 1-, 7-, and 30-day demand lags. Training covers days 31 to 640. The final 90 days are evaluated as rolling one-step forecasts: each day uses demand observed through the preceding day, including realized test-period lags, and assumes that day’s promotion is known before forecasting. The fitted coefficients remain fixed. These are not 90-day-ahead forecasts issued together on day 640.








Figure 21.4: Demand forecasting with linear quantile regression. Top: Historical demand with trend and seasonality. Bottom: Out-of-sample forecasts showing P10, P50, P90 quantiles (fan chart).





The held-out results are mixed. The P10-P90 interval has 79.6% coverage against a nominal 80%, while P30-P70 has 33.7% against 40%. The median forecast has mean absolute error 21.94 units. One near-nominal aggregate coverage rate does not establish calibration across quantiles, products, or promotional conditions.
